Earlier projections had expected the range of $14 to $16.\\n\\nLast month, Snap filed paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission to become a publicly traded company.\\n\\nSnap's Snapchat app is best known for disappearing messages and quirky facial filters for jazzing up selfies. It's popular with teenagers and younger millennials.\\n\\nBut despite Snapchat's popularity, user growth has slowed recently.\\n\\nSnapchat started 2017 with 158 million daily active users, most of whom are people in their teens, 20s and early 30s.\\n\\nDoes Snapchat need to go beyond young users to succeed?\\n\\nLaVon Murphy, 45, a photographer in Portland, Ore., told The Associated Press that she uses Snapchat to stay in touch with her 17-year-old son.\\n\\n\\\" 'I don't really understand why he and his friends use the app so extensively, but I am trying to keep up,' she said.\\n\\n\\\" \"---\\ntitle: Number of ChatGPT Users (March 2025)\\nauthor: Fabio Duarte\\ndate: 2025-06-05\\n---\\nNumber of ChatGPT Users (March 2025)\\n\\nOpenAI's ChatGPT took off in record-breaking fashion.\\n\\nThe artificial intelligence chatbot picked up millions of users in a very short space of time.\\n\\nToday, ChatGPT is the generic name for several large language models from OpenAI, including GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, and GPT-4.5.\\n\\nIn this up-to-date article, we'll explore just how many users ChatGPT currently has and other relevant data about the fast-growing AI platform.\\n\\nTop ChatGPT User Statistics\\n\\n- In just 5 days, ChatGPT surpassed 1 million users.\\n\\n- ChatGPT.com gets approximately 5.19 billion visits per month.\\n\\n- Around 62% of ChatGPT's social media traffic comes via YouTube.\\n\\n- Around 15% of ChatGPT's users are American.\\n\\n- More than 45% of ChatGPT users are under the age of 25.\\n\\n- OpenAI hopes to reach 1 billion users by the end of 2025.\\n\\nHow Many ChatGPT Users Are There?\\n\\nBased on February 2025 data from Semrush, ChatGPT ranks #8 in the world's most visited websites.\\n\\nAccording to Brad Lightcap, OpenAI's Chief Operating Officer, ChatGPT has 400 million weekly users. It plans to hit 1 billion users by the end of 2025.\\n\\n| Month | Weekly Users |\\n\\n| November 2022 | 1 million |\\n\\n| January 2023 | 30 million |\\n\\n| November 2023 | 100 million |\\n\\n| December 2024 | 300 million |\\n\\n| February 2025 | 400 million |\\n\\nSources: Reuters, Semrush, CNBC, The Verge, Techerati\\n\\nChatGPT User Demographics\\n\\n64.32% of ChatGPT users are male, and 35.68% are female.\\n\\nMore than 45% of its users are under the age of 25.\\n\\nSourc\", \"total_chars\": 10477, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"81520\", \"url\": \"https://www.businessofapps.com/data/tik-tok-statistics/\", \"score\": 0.4959165155887604, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: TikTok Revenue and Usage Statistics (2025)\\ndate: 2025-02-25\\n---\\nTikTok, known as Douyin in its home market, was launched in China in September 2016. It quickly started to gain traction in China and parent company ByteDance launched an international version the following year.\\n\\nOriginally launched as a short-form video sharing platform, primarily for lipsyncing and dancing videos, TikTok has grown into a fully-fledged video service with content available for all types of viewers.\\n\\nByteDance had prior experience on running wildly popular apps, as the operator of AI-powered news aggregation platform Toutiao. Zhang Yiming, the founder of ByteDance, incorporated a similar AI-model into TikTok, which is able to identify a user's interests and feed them more relevant videos.\\n\\nWhile many Chinese apps have failed to succeed outside of China, most notably Tencent's WeChat, TikTok managed to push itself into the overseas market through the acquisition of Musical.ly in November 2017 for $1 billion. This added 80 million users, mostly in the US, which TikTok then imported to its own platform.\\n\\nFrom there, TikTok snowballed into the most popular app in 2019 and 2020. It was downloaded 693 million times in 2019 and 850 million times in 2020. Even though it only launched in 2017, TikTok was the seventh-most downloaded app of the 2010s, and is one of the few competitors to Meta's dominance in social media.\\n\\nEven with this stellar growth, TikTok has faced several controversies. In this report, we share some of the biggest social media IPOs that the stock markets have seen and analyse their post-IPO performances.\\n\\nMeta Platforms (formerly Facebook) is one of the most successful social media IPOs in the past 15 years. Debuting in May 2012 at $38 per share, the company has seen strong growth since then.\\n\\nAll-time stock performance of Meta | Image credit: TradingView\\n\\nCurrently, META shares trade at around $507 each, representing a remarkable increase of 1,107 per cent. This surge implies that an initial investment of $10,000 in Meta's IPO would now exceed $120,000.\\n\\nOn November 7, 2013, Twitter initiated its IPO on the NYSE under the ticker symbol TWTR. Co-founders Dorsey, Williams, and Costolo collectively saw their wealth soar to $4 billion when the IPO priced at $26 reached $45.10 on the first day.\\n\\nElon Musk acquired Twitter in 2022 | Ima\", \"total_chars\": 4757, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"54725\", \"url\": \"https://www.businessofapps.com/data/facebook-statistics/\", \"score\": 0.4883835017681122, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Facebook Revenue and Usage Statistics (2025)\\ndate: 2025-02-20\\n---\\nFacebook probably needs no introduction; nonetheless, here is a quick history of the company.\\n\\nThe world's biggest and most-famous social network was launched by Mark Zuckerberg while he was a student at Harvard University, in early 2004. TheFacebook, as it was then known, was originally intended to serve a digitised version of the 'face books' held by Harvard's various colleges, which were paper directories containing images and personal information about students.\\n\\nInitially limited to Harvard, Facebook expanded to include students at other elite US universities, before branching out to all universities and high schools in the US and Canada. In 2006, it was finally decided to open the site up to the general public.\\n\\nTurn installs into active and engaged customers\\n\\nGrow in-app revenue and build user loyalty with custom retargeting and churn prediction campaigns from Adikteev.\\n\\nGet startedOver the years Facebook has expanded to include multimedia content and sharing content initially posted by others on Facebook or elsewhere. All stuff that seems rudimentary to us now, but at the time were pioneering innovations from Facebook and other members of that first post-MySpace wave of social networks.\\n\\nPrivate message functionality eventually became standalone app, Facebook Messenger, though is still part of the desktop site. (Sensor Tower began its app analysis on that date.)\\n\\nA number of apps from Google, the developer of Android, including Gmail and YouTube, have amassed over 5 billion downloads, but they ship pre-installed on most Android smartphones and tables.\\n\\nTikTok's 2 billion download milestone, a key metric to assess an app's growth, comes five months after it surpassed 1.5 billion downloads.\\n\\nIn the quarter that ended on March 31, TikTok was downloaded 315 million times — the highest number of downloads for any app in a quarter and — surpassing its previous best of 205.7 million downloads in Q4 2018.       "text": "---\ntitle: Here's Who Has Gone Public In 2019 (So Far)\nauthor: Alex Wilhelm\ndate: 2019-08-22\n---\nWelcome to our regularly-updated look at tech, tech-ish, and other venture-backed IPOs that took place on US exchanges in 2019. IPO dates largely refer to the day a company priced (sold) its IPO shares. Valuation data unless otherwise noted via Crunchbase.\n\nLast updated September 18, 2019.\n\nCloudflare\n\n- IPO date: September 13, 2019\n\n- IPO price: $15 per share\n\n- IPO valuation: $4.4 billion\n\n- Initial post-IPO arc: Positive.\n\nCloudflare finally settled on pricing its shares at $15 after previously setting ranges of $10 to $12 and then $12 to $14. Its IPO was a success, with its stock opening at $18 on its first day of trading. Things are still going strong, with its stock trading at $19.34 as of midday September 18.\n\nSmileDirectClub\n\n- IPO date: September 12, 2019\n\n- IPO price: $23 per share\n\n- IPO valuation: $8.9 billion\n\n- Initial post-IPO arc: Down.\n\nDIY teeth straightening company SmileDirectClub set its IPO price at $23, above the price range of $19 to $22 the company had intended. But pricing high has its consequences, and nearly a week after beginning trading on the public markets, SmileDirectClub's stock still hasn't hit $23. Its shares closed at $16.67 on its first day of trading, and is at $19.07 as of midday September 17.\n\n9F\n\n- IPO date: August 15, 2019\n\n- IPO price: $9.50 per share\n",

(Sensor Tower began its app analysis on that date.)\\n\\nA number of apps from Google, the developer of Android, including Gmail and YouTube, have amassed over 5 billion downloads, but they ship pre-installed on most Android smartphones and tables.\\n\\nTikTok's 2 billion download milestone, a key metric to assess an app's growth, comes five months after it surpassed 1.5 billion downloads.\\n\\nIn the quarter that ended on March 31, TikTok was downloaded 315 million times — the highest number of downloads for any app in a quarter and — surpassing its previous best of 205.7 million downloads in Q4 2018. Adhanom's favorite piece is the shorts because they're personalized and\", \"total_chars\": 4045, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"88329\", \"url\": \"https://www.graduatefashionfoundation.com/news/how-designer-claire-barrow-launched-a-label-before-graduation-ph8y6\", \"score\": 0.5883802175521851, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: How Claire Barrow Launched Her Label While at University\\nauthor: Dom Libert\\ndate: 2019-06-18\\n---\\nIt goes without saying, starting your own label fresh out of university is easier said than done. Young designers are often discouraged from launching a brand before cutting their teeth in the industry, gaining the experience, maturity and acumen needed to survive as a business owner.\\n\\nClaire Barrow, a young London designer, is an exception to the rule. Claire has recently made it clear she refuses to conform with the traditional fashion schedule, showing her designs outside the seasonal timeline.\\n\\nBelow, she shares her advice with GFW contributor Sara Liberati for starting a brand out of university, diversifying your skill set for the future of the industry, and staying true to yourself.\\n\\nHi Claire! Can you tell us a bit more about your experience launching your label? How and when did it come about?\\n\\nI attended the University of Westminster in 2008, moving to London from the North East of England, and there I took the option to do four years, so that I could do a year out. During that year, I tried a few internships, but I mainly wanted to start work within the industry on my own, so I started doing custom painted items for my friends, and that gradually led to creating clothes for magazines and celebrities as well.\\n\\nI then did a capsule collection for the shop Joseph, and then went\", \"total_chars\": 8691, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"72972\", \"url\": \"https://www.nssmag.com/en/fashion/36100/community-fashion-places-faces-corteiz\", \"score\": 0.56876140832901, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why communities are so important for brands\\nauthor: Author Sagra de Manueles\\ndate: 2024-03-14\\n---\\nWhy communities are so important for brands\\n\\nBorn in the streetwear world, luxury fashion also wants to recreate them\\n\\nMarch 14th, 2024\\n\\nPossessing its own community is something fundamental for any fashion brand - even though the meaning of the word is often ambiguous. In the best cases, a brand's community forms mostly on its own, albeit with the help and encouragement of the brand itself, as is the case with Diesel, for example; there are many others, especially in the luxury field, where the community and the clientele do not always correspond, leading us to speak more of a \\\"following\\\" than a community, which is more artificially constructed through precise marketing strategies. Either way, a community is needed because it constitutes not so much the audience of a brand, but the people who are under its influence. If a certain collection or brand launches a trend that others follow, think of Miu Miu or Balenciaga in recent years, it is the community that acts as a sounding board for it - what in marketing theory is called \\\"early adopters\\\". Communities play a crucial role in defining a brand identity: the progressive ladies of the 1920s were the community of Chanel, just as CEOs and magnates from around the world represent the community of Brunello Cucinelli or Loro Piana, rock singers are the community of any Hedi Slimane project, and career women with an intellectual side are the community of The Row and Phoebe Philo.         "content": "[{\"docid\": \"72972\", \"url\": \"https://www.nssmag.com/en/fashion/36100/community-fashion-places-faces-corteiz\", \"score\": 0.5958995819091797, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why communities are so important for brands\\nauthor: Author Sagra de Manueles\\ndate: 2024-03-14\\n---\\nWhy communities are so important for brands\\n\\nBorn in the streetwear world, luxury fashion also wants to recreate them\\n\\nMarch 14th, 2024\\n\\nPossessing its own community is something fundamental for any fashion brand - even though the meaning of the word is often ambiguous. In the best cases, a brand's community forms mostly on its own, albeit with the help and encouragement of the brand itself, as is the case with Diesel, for example; there are many others, especially in the luxury field, where the community and the clientele do not always correspond, leading us to speak more of a \\\"following\\\" than a community, which is more artificially constructed through precise marketing strategies. Either way, a community is needed because it constitutes not so much the audience of a brand, but the people who are under its influence. If a certain collection or brand launches a trend that others follow, think of Miu Miu or Balenciaga in recent years, it is the community that acts as a sounding board for it - what in marketing theory is called \\\"early adopters\\\". Communities play a crucial role in defining a brand identity: the progressive ladies of the 1920s were the community of Chanel, just as CEOs and magnates from around the world represent the community of Brunello Cucinelli or Loro Piana, rock singers are the community of any Hedi Slimane project, and career women with an intellectual side are the community of The Row and Phoebe Philo. Crucially, participants were required to wear their (clean) jeans to the event, hand them in, and wa\", \"total_chars\": 10903, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"93766\", \"url\": \"https://moresneakers.com/blog/detail/corteiz:-the-guerilla-streetwear-brand-that-took-over-london\", \"score\": 0.5700938701629639, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Corteiz: The Guerilla Streetwear Brand That Took Over London\\ndate: 2023-04-12\\n---\\nCorteiz's Unconventional Marketing Tactics\\n\\nIn recent years, it has become rarer to see hordes of shoppers mobbing city streets to buy a limited edition drop from any streetwear label. Many streetwear brands have followed the same playbook - design a seasonal collection, schedule an online release date, and continue selling items via stockists or other retail partners. However, there are brands like Corteiz that have employed unconventional guerilla marketing tactics to capture hype and allure unseen within streetwear in some time.\\n\\nFounded in 2017 by Clint Ogbenna, a British-Nigerian entrepreneur, Corteiz RTW (Rules The World) has become one of the most popular streetwear brands to come out of London since Palace. As these ethical concerns gain prominence, the concept of community clothing has evolved into something far more than just a trend. Community clothing is now a multifaceted approach to fashion, with each initiative having its own unique impact.\\n\\nIn this article, we explore the diverse landscape of community clothing, with a special focus on those that advocate for sustainability and drive positive change.\\n\\nBrand Communities vs. Community Clothing: Unpacking the Connection\\n\\nA concept closely related to community clothing is brand communities, often mistaken for the same thing. The collective value both terms bring to the table lies in the creation of implicit, discursive, and emotional value for consumers [1]. This overlap can create some confusion. Brand communities aim to strengthen the consumer-brand relationship while fostering a sense of loyalty and understanding between consumers and the community [2,3].\\n\\nThis creates a shared identity and a deeper connection with the brand's vision, turning consumers into \\\"co-creators\\\" of the products [3] or, at the very least, making them feel that their voices and desires influence the brand's projects.\\n\\nSo, what exactly is comm\", \"total_chars\": 15642, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"9472\", \"url\": \"https://www.stu.edu/news/flysupply-stu-fashion-collab-launch/\", \"score\": 0.5577812194824219, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: FlySupply & STU Fashion Collab Launch\\ndate: 2023-10-24\\n---\\nFlySupply & STU Fashion Collab Launch\\n\\nby Walter Villa, Special to STU\\n\\nThis was a match made in heaven – literally.\\n\\nSt. Thomas University, a Catholic institution, and Fly Supply, a clothing line with religious messaging, have made a collaboration blessed by the angels.\\n\\nOn Friday afternoon – accented by a live DJ and tasty food and beverages — students and other guests ventured out to the on-campus Fernandez Family Center lobby to enjoy the launch of Fly Supply's STU line. There's the celebrity designer, which could either mean a celebrity-turned-designer or a designer-turned-celebrity; the socialite designer; the influencer designer (again, that could be an influencer-turned-designer or vice versa); the millennial 'Girlboss' founder; the mythical, legendary designer whose name is everywhere but whose personal life and personality we know little about. With decreasing frequency, it seems, there's also the talented, classically trained, dues-paid, behind-the-scenes designer who wants their work to speak for itself.\\n\\nFashion brands have been harnessing the power of celebrity for over a century. In the best cases, a brand's community forms mostly on its own, albeit with the help and encouragement of the brand itself, as is the case with Diesel, for example; there are many others, especially in the luxury field, where the community and the clientele do not always correspond, leading us to speak more of a \\\"following\\\" than a community, which is more artificially constructed through precise marketing strategies. Either way, a community is needed because it constitutes not so much the audience of a brand, but the people who are under its influence. If a certain collection or brand launches a trend that others follow, think of Miu Miu or Balenciaga in recent years, it is the community that acts as a sounding board for it - what in marketing theory is called \\\"early adopters\\\".         "content": "[{\"docid\": \"77382\", \"url\": \"https://www.businessofapps.com/data/spotify-statistics/\", \"score\": 0.7166255712509155, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Spotify Revenue and Usage Statistics (2025)\\ndate: 2025-02-25\\n---\\nSpotify is the world's biggest music streaming platform by number of subscribers. Users of the service simply need to register to have access to one of the largest collections of music in history, plus podcasts and other audio content.\\n\\nIt operates on a freemium model. Free Spotify access comes with lower sound quality, advertisements and requires an internet connection. Those who pay for Spotify Premium can listen uninterrupted to high-quality recordings and are able to download songs for offline listening.\\n\\nSpotify was founded in 2006 in Stockholm, Sweden, by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. The two wanted to create a legal digital music platform to respond to growing challenge of online music piracy in the early 2000s.\\n\\nEventually convincing record labels to agree to share content in return for an aggregate 20 percent stake, Spotify was launched in 2008. It was an instant success, with a Facebook partnership helping it rise rapidly to prominence. Surviving the transition to mobile, Spotify went public in April 2018, with a market cap of $26.5 billion after the first day of trading.\\n\\nIt has drawn criticism from recording artists, who complain that it pays too little. Gucci\\n\\nGetty Images\\n\\nGuccio Gucci opened a small saddlery shop in 1906 and started selling practical leather bags to his horsemen customers sometime in the '20s. Erling Persson wanted to make great fashion available and affordable to everyone and do this in the right way. From a single store in 1947 we became a family of brands offering fashion and design to customers worldwide. This is our story.\\n\\nThe '40s and '50s\\n\\n1947\\n\\nInspired by his trip to New York City the year before, Swedish entrepreneur Erling Persson opens a new womenswear store in Västerås, Sweden. Awarded the Perry Ellis Gold Thimble Award and the prestigious Design Student of the Year Award, Jacobs displayed his unique talent from the very beginning.\\n\\nIt was around this time Jacobs aligned with his business partner Robert Duffy. After more than two decades, the two are still collaborative associates. In 1986, the first clothing line with the Marc Jacobs label was released. The line was such an instant success that 1987 brought Jacobs another highly distinguished honor: the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA) Perry Ellis Award for New Fashion Talent.\\n\\nQuickly working up the fashion chain, Jacobs and Duffy began working with Tristan Russo in 1989.         "content": "[{\"docid\": \"72972\", \"url\": \"https://www.nssmag.com/en/fashion/36100/community-fashion-places-faces-corteiz\", \"score\": 0.5958995819091797, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why communities are so important for brands\\nauthor: Author Sagra de Manueles\\ndate: 2024-03-14\\n---\\nWhy communities are so important for brands\\n\\nBorn in the streetwear world, luxury fashion also wants to recreate them\\n\\nMarch 14th, 2024\\n\\nPossessing its own community is something fundamental for any fashion brand - even though the meaning of the word is often ambiguous. In the best cases, a brand's community forms mostly on its own, albeit with the help and encouragement of the brand itself, as is the case with Diesel, for example; there are many others, especially in the luxury field, where the community and the clientele do not always correspond, leading us to speak more of a \\\"following\\\" than a community, which is more artificially constructed through precise marketing strategies. Either way, a community is needed because it constitutes not so much the audience of a brand, but the people who are under its influence. If a certain collection or brand launches a trend that others follow, think of Miu Miu or Balenciaga in recent years, it is the community that acts as a sounding board for it - what in marketing theory is called \\\"early adopters\\\". Communities play a crucial role in defining a brand identity: the progressive ladies of the 1920s were the community of Chanel, just as CEOs and magnates from around the world represent the community of Brunello Cucinelli or Loro Piana, rock singers are the community of any Hedi Slimane project, and career women with an intellectual side are the community of The Row and Phoebe Philo. There is a clear connection, however, betwee\", \"total_chars\": 5831, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"22731\", \"url\": \"https://www.voguebusiness.com/fashion/corteiz-clint-and-the-future-of-streetwear\", \"score\": 0.573395311832428, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why everyone's talking about Corteiz\\nauthor: Kati Chitrakorn\\ndate: 2022-01-31\\n---\\nTo receive the Vogue Business newsletter, sign up here.\\n\\nOn a weekend in January, groups of young people were spotted climbing fences and running through a car park in Wormwood Scrubs, west London, carrying puffer jackets from brands including The North Face, Stussy, Moncler, Supreme and Arc'teryx. They were following clues to take part in Da Great Bolo Exchange, an event organised by London-based streetwear brand Corteiz. Coordinates were shared on social media along with instructions to bring an authentic branded down jacket in reasonable condition. That made you eligible to receive one of Corteiz's new Bolo jackets. Hundreds of young adults showed up, even though the brand had only 50 jackets to give away.\\n\\nCorteiz (also known as Crtz) was launched in 2017. The founder is known publicly as simply Clint. His pieces — including £30 t-shirts, £120 joggers and £125 cargos — feature a distinctive Alcatraz logo that represents rebellion against convention, considered the core message behind the brand.\\n\\nPieces tend to sell out within minutes. The brand produces a limited run of each product, sold via a private e-commerce site (only those selected are granted access via a password) or at a surprise drop in the physical world. The Instagram account is also private. Resale is discouraged by Corteiz, but difficult to enforce — Bolo jackets are retailing on Depop for £500.\\n\\nClint himself declined to speak with Vogue Business for this story and rarely speaks to press, but it's important not t\", \"total_chars\": 9174, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"69364\", \"url\": \"https://www.gq.com/story/corteiz-brooklyn-denim-exchange-scene-report\", \"score\": 0.5704416632652283, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Inside Corteiz's Frenzied Brooklyn Denim Exchange\\nauthor: Jordan Coley\\ndate: 2024-05-16\\n---\\nOn most Saturday mornings, the post-industrial, post-gentrification blocks of northwest Greenpoint belong to the stroller pushers, the brunchers, the Alo-clad joggers. This particular Saturday is only slightly different. The women in fleeces and leggings toting fiddle leafs from the plant store and the young parents taxiing toddlers to Transmitter Park are there, yes. Community clothing is now a multifaceted approach to fashion, with each initiative having its own unique impact.\\n\\nIn this article, we explore the diverse landscape of community clothing, with a special focus on those that advocate for sustainability and drive positive change.\\n\\nBrand Communities vs. Community Clothing: Unpacking the Connection\\n\\nA concept closely related to community clothing is brand communities, often mistaken for the same thing. With decreasing frequency, it seems, there's also the talented, classically trained, dues-paid, behind-the-scenes designer who wants their work to speak for itself.\\n\\nFashion brands have been harnessing the power of celebrity for over a century. Ove\", \"total_chars\": 2997, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"22731\", \"url\": \"https://www.voguebusiness.com/fashion/corteiz-clint-and-the-future-of-streetwear\", \"score\": 0.6766314506530762, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why everyone's talking about Corteiz\\nauthor: Kati Chitrakorn\\ndate: 2022-01-31\\n---\\nTo receive the Vogue Business newsletter, sign up here.\\n\\nOn a weekend in January, groups of young people were spotted climbing fences and running through a car park in Wormwood Scrubs, west London, carrying puffer jackets from brands including The North Face, Stussy, Moncler, Supreme and Arc'teryx. In the best cases, a brand's community forms mostly on its own, albeit with the help and encouragement of the brand itself, as is the case with Diesel, for example; there are many others, especially in the luxury field, where the community and the clientele do not always correspond, leading us to speak more of a \\\"following\\\" than a community, which is more artificially constructed through precise marketing strategies. Adhanom's favorite piece is the shorts because they're personalized and\", \"total_chars\": 4045, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"28383\", \"url\": \"https://www.voguebusiness.com/fashion/how-represent-went-from-a-garden-shed-to-50-million-in-sales\", \"score\": 0.45833244919776917, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: How Represent went from a garden shed to £50 million in sales\\nauthor: Lucy Maguire\\ndate: 2023-05-23\\n---\\nTo receive the Vogue Business newsletter, sign up here.\\n\\nBrothers George and Michael Heaton started printing T-shirts in their bedrooms while both studying graphic design at Salford University in Manchester, England, in 2011. Now, despite a saturated contemporary menswear market dominated by the likes of Palm Angels, Ami Paris and Fear of God, Represent's annual revenue has hit almost £50 million — and, spurred by international expansion, new categories and a new company structure, its founders believe it could reach £250 million by 2025.\\n\\n\\\"We've been working for 12 years and now the dream is actually happening,\\\" says George, speaking from Represent's sales showroom in East London, where buyers peruse the Spring/Summer 2024 collection, comprising signature hoodies, graphic T-shirts, denim and footwear. \\\"It still doesn't feel like real life.\\\"\\n\\nRepresent is a contemporary menswear label inspired by rock music and LA skate culture.         "content": "[{\"docid\": \"72972\", \"url\": \"https://www.nssmag.com/en/fashion/36100/community-fashion-places-faces-corteiz\", \"score\": 0.5958995819091797, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why communities are so important for brands\\nauthor: Author Sagra de Manueles\\ndate: 2024-03-14\\n---\\nWhy communities are so important for brands\\n\\nBorn in the streetwear world, luxury fashion also wants to recreate them\\n\\nMarch 14th, 2024\\n\\nPossessing its own community is something fundamental for any fashion brand - even though the meaning of the word is often ambiguous. In the best cases, a brand's community forms mostly on its own, albeit with the help and encouragement of the brand itself, as is the case with Diesel, for example; there are many others, especially in the luxury field, where the community and the clientele do not always correspond, leading us to speak more of a \\\"following\\\" than a community, which is more artificially constructed through precise marketing strategies. Either way, a community is needed because it constitutes not so much the audience of a brand, but the people who are under its influence. If a certain collection or brand launches a trend that others follow, think of Miu Miu or Balenciaga in recent years, it is the community that acts as a sounding board for it - what in marketing theory is called \\\"early adopters\\\". Communities play a crucial role in defining a brand identity: the progressive ladies of the 1920s were the community of Chanel, just as CEOs and magnates from around the world represent the community of Brunello Cucinelli or Loro Piana, rock singers are the community of any Hedi Slimane project, and career women with an intellectual side are the community of The Row and Phoebe Philo. There is a clear connection, however, betwee\", \"total_chars\": 5831, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"22731\", \"url\": \"https://www.voguebusiness.com/fashion/corteiz-clint-and-the-future-of-streetwear\", \"score\": 0.573395311832428, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why everyone's talking about Corteiz\\nauthor: Kati Chitrakorn\\ndate: 2022-01-31\\n---\\nTo receive the Vogue Business newsletter, sign up here.\\n\\nOn a weekend in January, groups of young people were spotted climbing fences and running through a car park in Wormwood Scrubs, west London, carrying puffer jackets from brands including The North Face, Stussy, Moncler, Supreme and Arc'teryx. They were following clues to take part in Da Great Bolo Exchange, an event organised by London-based streetwear brand Corteiz. Coordinates were shared on social media along with instructions to bring an authentic branded down jacket in reasonable condition. That made you eligible to receive one of Corteiz's new Bolo jackets. Hundreds of young adults showed up, even though the brand had only 50 jackets to give away.\\n\\nCorteiz (also known as Crtz) was launched in 2017. The founder is known publicly as simply Clint. His pieces — including £30 t-shirts, £120 joggers and £125 cargos — feature a distinctive Alcatraz logo that represents rebellion against convention, considered the core message behind the brand.\\n\\nPieces tend to sell out within minutes. The brand produces a limited run of each product, sold via a private e-commerce site (only those selected are granted access via a password) or at a surprise drop in the physical world. The Instagram account is also private. This particular Saturday is only slightly different. The women in fleeces and leggings toting fiddle leafs from the plant store and the young parents taxiing toddlers to Transmitter Park are there, yes. So too, however, are about 400 anxious 13 to 30 year olds, clamoring for the opportunity to give their pants away.\\n\\nAt about 11 a.m. on a block of West Street just south of Greenpoint Avenue, the air fills with the sound of skidding Citi Bike tires and recently released Air Jordans thudding against the pavement. Suddenly, frantically, a line is forming outside a nondescript warehouse. \\\"DA GREAT DENIM EXCHANGE,\\\" a pop-up event orchestrated by British streetwear label Corteiz, is about to begin—and it's bringing a bit of streetwear hysteria into the neighborhood's millennial equanimity.\\n\\nA day earlier, the brand announced via Instagram that in less than 24 hours it would be doing its second-ever event in New York. According to the post, the first 300 people to arrive and turn in jeans from a select list of brands (\\\"LEVI'S 501s - TRUE RELIGION - CARHARTT JEANS/CARPENTERS - DICKIES - TOMMY HILFIGER - RALPH LAUREN - CALVIN KLEINS - S😜PREME - STUSSY - PALACE - AMIRI\\\") would receive a pair of Corteiz denim in return. Crucially, participants were required to wear their (clean) jeans to the event, hand them in, and wa\", \"total_chars\": 10903, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"93766\", \"url\": \"https://moresneakers.com/blog/detail/corteiz:-the-guerilla-streetwear-brand-that-took-over-london\", \"score\": 0.5700938701629639, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Corteiz: The Guerilla Streetwear Brand That Took Over London\\ndate: 2023-04-12\\n---\\nCorteiz's Unconventional Marketing Tactics\\n\\nIn recent years, it has become rarer to see hordes of shoppers mobbing city streets to buy a limited edition drop from any streetwear label. Many streetwear brands have followed the same playbook - design a seasonal collection, schedule an online release date, and continue selling items via stockists or other retail partners. However, there are brands like Corteiz that have employed unconventional guerilla marketing tactics to capture hype and allure unseen within streetwear in some time.\\n\\nFounded in 2017 by Clint Ogbenna, a British-Nigerian entrepreneur, Corteiz RTW (Rules The World) has become one of the most popular streetwear brands to come out of London since Palace. Within the past five years, the brand's logo of Alcatraz Island has blown up and is now spotted everywhere. The brand's garments have been frequently sighted on UK rap stars such as Central Cee, slowthai, Stormzy, and Dave.\\n\\nCorteiz has gained recognition for its garments among UK rap stars including Central Cee, slowthai, Stormzy, and Dave. In addition, some of the biggest celebrities have given their seal of approval to the brand. Recently, Drake was seen sporting a leather jacket that the brand released this winter, and Pharrell invited the brand's founder, Clint, to a private Friendsgiving dinner held at Selfridges last fall.\\n\\nSurprisingly, Corteiz's social media pages were originally private - for a while, new customers could only learn about the brand's latest relea\", \"total_chars\": 3490, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"37360\", \"url\": \"https://ecoaya.com/blogs/sustainability/community-clothing-brand-communities-sustainable-fashion\", \"score\": 0.5627676248550415, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Community Clothing: Redefining Fashion for a Sustainable Future\\ndate: 2024-10-01\\n---\\nCommunity Clothing:\\n\\nRedefining Fashion for a Sustainable Future\\n\\n.\\n\\nAYA | JANUARY 14, 2025\\n\\nREADING TIME: 7 minutes\\n\\nToday, the fashion industry faces challenges not only from the economic and environmental impacts of fast fashion but also from growing ethical debates that influence consumer purchasing behaviors. As these ethical concerns gain prominence, the concept of community clothing has evolved into something far more than just a trend. Community clothing is now a multifaceted approach to fashion, with each initiative having its own unique impact.\\n\\nIn this article, we explore the diverse landscape of community clothing, with a special focus on those that advocate for sustainability and drive positive change.\\n\\nBrand Communities vs. Community Clothing: Unpacking the Connection\\n\\nA concept closely related to community clothing is brand communities, often mistaken for the same thing. The collective value both terms bring to the table lies in the creation of implicit, discursive, and emotional value for consumers [1]. This overlap can create some confusion. Brand communities aim to strengthen the consumer-brand relationship while fostering a sense of loyalty and understanding between consumers and the community [2,3].\\n\\nThis creates a shared identity and a deeper connection with the brand's vision, turning consumers into \\\"co-creators\\\" of the products [3] or, at the very least, making them feel that their voices and desires influence the brand's projects.\\n\\nSo, what exactly is comm\", \"total_chars\": 15642, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"9472\", \"url\": \"https://www.stu.edu/news/flysupply-stu-fashion-collab-launch/\", \"score\": 0.5577812194824219, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: FlySupply & STU Fashion Collab Launch\\ndate: 2023-10-24\\n---\\nFlySupply & STU Fashion Collab Launch\\n\\nby Walter Villa, Special to STU\\n\\nThis was a match made in heaven – literally.\\n\\nSt. Thomas University, a Catholic institution, and Fly Supply, a clothing line with religious messaging, have made a collaboration blessed by the angels.\\n\\nOn Friday afternoon – accented by a live DJ and tasty food and beverages — students and other guests ventured out to the on-campus Fernandez Family Center lobby to enjoy the launch of Fly Supply's STU line. The sporty line, in an array of bright colors, features messages such as:\\n\\n\\\"GOD GOT MY BACK.\\\"\\n\\n\\\"NEVER SOLD MY SOUL.\\\"\\n\\nAnd …\\n\\n\\\"THE DEVIL IS JEALOUS OF ME.\\\"\\n\\nProfessor Ashlee Rzyczycki, the director of STU's fashion merchandising program, said it was in 2021 that she met the four founders of Fly Supply – Garrett Brown, Rick Maxwell, Kevin Pamphile, and Reginald Bourdeau, all of whom are from Miami.\\n\\nProfessor Rzyczycki quickly decided that working with this hip quartet of designers would be a huge win for St. Thomas University in general, and her students in particular.\\n\\n\\\"They have a great brand,\\\" said Professor Rzyczycki, who was introduced to the Fly Supply guys by STU employee Brandon Vega. \\\"I wanted to incorporate that brand into my classroom.\\\"\\n\\nIn that initial meeting, Professor Rzyczycki said she had an \\\"amazing\\\" two-hour conversation with the Fly Supply guys.\\n\\n\\\"Their brand is super successful,\\\" she said. \\\"I knew this collaboration would really resonate with my students.\\\"\\n\\nFly Supply has previously collaborated with Miami Heat leg\", \"total_chars\": 3707, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"89023\", \"url\": \"https://fashionista.com/2020/08/fashion-brands-celebrity-famous-public-facing-founders\", \"score\": 0.5567072033882141, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Does a Fashion Brand Need a Public-Facing Founder to Survive?\\nauthor: Dhani Mau\\ndate: 2020-08-04\\n---\\nDoes a Fashion Brand Need a Public-Facing Founder to Survive?\\n\\nIn the fashion world, there are a smorgasbord of founders and designers we read and hear about. There's the celebrity designer, which could either mean a celebrity-turned-designer or a designer-turned-celebrity; the socialite designer; the influencer designer (again, that could be an influencer-turned-designer or vice versa); the millennial 'Girlboss' founder; the mythical, legendary designer whose name is everywhere but whose personal life and personality we know little about. With decreasing frequency, it seems, there's also the talented, classically trained, dues-paid, behind-the-scenes designer who wants their work to speak for itself.\\n\\nFashion brands have been harnessing the power of celebrity for over a century. But the \\\"celebrity brand\\\" as we know it really gained traction around the late '90s and early 2000s, thanks to stars like Jay-Z, Sean Combs, Jessica Simpson and more pushing lesser-known names off the sales floor at major retailers like Macy's and upending the entire industry in the process. Ove\", \"total_chars\": 2997, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"22731\", \"url\": \"https://www.voguebusiness.com/fashion/corteiz-clint-and-the-future-of-streetwear\", \"score\": 0.6766314506530762, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why everyone's talking about Corteiz\\nauthor: Kati Chitrakorn\\ndate: 2022-01-31\\n---\\nTo receive the Vogue Business newsletter, sign up here.\\n\\nOn a weekend in January, groups of young people were spotted climbing fences and running through a car park in Wormwood Scrubs, west London, carrying puffer jackets from brands including The North Face, Stussy, Moncler, Supreme and Arc'teryx. In the best cases, a brand's community forms mostly on its own, albeit with the help and encouragement of the brand itself, as is the case with Diesel, for example; there are many others, especially in the luxury field, where the community and the clientele do not always correspond, leading us to speak more of a \\\"following\\\" than a community, which is more artificially constructed through precise marketing strategies. Either way, a community is needed because it constitutes not so much the audience of a brand, but the people who are under its influence. If a certain collection or brand launches a trend that others follow, think of Miu Miu or Balenciaga in recent years, it is the community that acts as a sounding board for it - what in marketing theory is called \\\"early adopters\\\". Few startups went public, and a horde of richly-valued unicorns sat on the sidelines simply waiting.\\n\\nHappily, for investors and founders alike, 2018 has produced a host of technology IPOs. In fact, the flow of tech companies going public was a theme in our Q1 venture reporting and our Q2 venture reporting. In the middle of the year, it was plain that things were going to stay hot, and despite a present pause, the rest of the year is looking busy on the IPO front.\\n\\nThis year has seen a host of Chinese companies going public domestically (here are a few stories on that), a brace of hardware IPOs, and SaaS has done well in terms of offerings, and results.\\n\\nThere have been a few misses, of course. Domo's hot mess forced it to give up most of its paper value. Meanwhile, M17 Entertainment struggled in its debut, with CEO ringing the bell and then announcing days later that the company had shelved its IPO.\\n\\nAll told, however, the year-to-date, domestic technology IPO list is getting long.         "content": "{\"docid\": \"77382\", \"url\": \"https://www.businessofapps.com/data/spotify-statistics/\", \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Spotify Revenue and Usage Statistics (2025)\\ndate: 2025-02-25\\n---\\nSpotify is the world's biggest music streaming platform by number of subscribers. Free Spotify access comes with lower sound quality, advertisements and requires an internet connection. Those who pay for Spotify Premium can listen uninterrupted to high-quality recordings and are able to download songs for offline listening.\\n\\nSpotify was founded in 2006 in Stockholm, Sweden, by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. The two wanted to create a legal digital music platform to respond to growing challenge of online music piracy in the early 2000s.\\n\\nEventually convincing record labels to agree to share content in return for an aggregate 20 percent stake, Spotify was launched in 2008. It was an instant success, with a Facebook partnership helping it rise rapidly to prominence. Surviving the transition to mobile, Spotify went public in April 2018, with a market cap of $26.5 billion after the first day of trading.\\n\\nIt has drawn criticism from recording artists, who complain that it pays too little. Claims to democratize the music industry have also been questioned, with the world's biggest four music labels responsible for 87 percent of content available on Spotify.\\n\\nUnfair or not, with the days of physical music long behind us (with the exception of vinyl junkies), Spotify dominates the way we consume music this century.         "content": "[{\"docid\": \"84696\", \"url\": \"https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2017/03/02/518081927/snapchat-parent-to-begin-trading-on-the-new-york-stock-exchange-thursday\", \"score\": 0.5952717065811157, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Snapchat Parent's Stock Soars By 50 Percent On First Day Of Trading\\nauthor: Doreen McCallister\\ndate: 2017-03-02\\n---\\nSnapchat Parent's Stock Soars By 50 Percent On First Day Of Trading\\n\\nShares of Snap Inc., parent of the popular disappearing-message and camera-centric app Snapchat, rose by more than $8 in the first hours of trading Thursday, as the company watched the $17 price of its initial public offering of 200 million nonvoting shares soar by 50 percent as of mid-day Thursday.\\n\\nThe stock opened above $24 when the new offering began sales shortly after 11 a.m. It then rose above $25 a share, hitting $25.64 by 1:31 p.m.\\n\\nThe initial pricing valued the 5-year-old company, based in Los Angeles, at $24 billion. Earlier projections had expected the range of $14 to $16.\\n\\nLast month, Snap filed paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission to become a publicly traded company.\\n\\nSnap's Snapchat app is best known for disappearing messages and quirky facial filters for jazzing up selfies. It's popular with teenagers and younger millennials.\\n\\nBut despite Snapchat's popularity, user growth has slowed recently.\\n\\nSnapchat started 2017 with 158 million daily active users, most of whom are people in their teens, 20s and early 30s.\\n\\nDoes Snapchat need to go beyond young users to succeed?\\n\\nLaVon Murphy, 45, a photographer in Portland, Ore., told The Associated Press that she uses Snapchat to stay in touch with her 17-year-old son.\\n\\n\\\" 'I don't really understand why he and his friends use the app so extensively, but I am trying to keep up,' she said.\\n\\n\\\" 'It allows me to be\", \"total_chars\": 3113, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"22806\", \"url\": \"https://www.statista.com/statistics/272014/global-social-networks-ranked-by-number-of-users/\", \"score\": 0.53764808177948, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Most used social networks 2025, by number of users\\nauthor: Stacy Jo Dixon; Mar\\ndate: 2025-03-26\\n---\\nMarket leader Facebook was the first social network to surpass one billion registered accounts and currently sits at more than three billion monthly active users. Meta Platforms owns four of the biggest social media platforms, all with more than one billion monthly active users each: Facebook (core platform), WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, and Instagram. In the third quarter of 2023, Facebook reported around four billion monthly core Family product users.\\n\\nThe United States and China account for the most high-profile social platforms\\n\\nMost top ranked social networks with more than 100 million users originated in the United States, but services like Chinese social networks WeChat, QQ or video sharing app Douyin have also garnered mainstream appeal in their respective regions due to local context and content. Douyin's popularity has led to the platform releasing an international version of its network: a little app called TikTok.\\n\\nHow many people use social media?\\n\\nThe leading social networks are usually available in multiple languages and enable users to connect with friends or people across geographical, political, or economic borders. In the best cases, a brand's community forms mostly on its own, albeit with the help and encouragement of the brand itself, as is the case with Diesel, for example; there are many others, especially in the luxury field, where the community and the clientele do not always correspond, leading us to speak more of a \\\"following\\\" than a community, which is more artificially constructed through precise marketing strategies. Either way, a community is needed because it constitutes not so much the audience of a brand, but the people who are under its influence. If a certain collection or brand launches a trend that others follow, think of Miu Miu or Balenciaga in recent years, it is the community that acts as a sounding board for it - what in marketing theory is called \\\"early adopters\\\". Communities play a crucial role in defining a brand identity: the progressive ladies of the 1920s were the community of Chanel, just as CEOs and magnates from around the world represent the community of Brunello Cucinelli or Loro Piana, rock singers are the community of any Hedi Slimane project, and career women with an intellectual side are the community of The Row and Phoebe Philo. There is a clear connection, however, betwee\", \"total_chars\": 5831, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"87070\", \"url\": \"https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbescommunicationscouncil/2024/10/01/the-power-of-community-how-fashion-brands-are-building-loyalty-among-gen-z/\", \"score\": 0.5429238677024841, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: The Power Of Community: How Fashion Brands Are Building Loyalty Among Gen Z\\ndate: 2024-10-01\\n---\\nAlison Bringé is Chief Marketing Officer at Launchmetrics, a leading Brand Performance Cloud in Fashion, Lifestyle and Beauty.\\n\\nWhat do Gen Z consumers want? There are many viable answers to that question, but I'd argue that it has less to do with the products that brands sell and more to do with the feelings they create.\\n\\nGen Zers want to make connections. They want to share and participate—to find meaning in a digital world. In short, they want to belong.\\n\\nFor fashion, lifestyle and beauty brands looking to win over Gen Z's loyalty, this is a crucial thing to understand. Gen Z consumers want to connect with others who share their values; they want to find their tribe—and the brands that succeed are the ones that step in and fill that need in an authentic way.\\n\\nWhy Is Community So Important?\\n\\nBelonging is at the crux of it, but there's more to be said about the importance of community. For one thing, Gen Zers prefer brands with stories; brands that stand for something—brands they can connect to on an emotional level. Purchasing from such brands goes beyond the product: It's a form of self-expression—a badge they wear to publicly demonstrate their values. Building a community around your brand allows Gen Z to know where you stand and to stand with you.\\n\\nAt the same time, the concept of authority has shifted.     "text": "Corteiz Rules the World, also known simply as Corteiz or CRTZ RTW, are a London based streetwear brand. The brand has grown meteorically since it's inception, highlighted by musical artists such as Stormzy, Dave and Drake seen sporting Corteiz items . Clint and Corteiz even gained recognition and support from the late designer Virgil Abloh, who transcended the fashion industry and is seen by many as one of the greatest designers in recent history .\nTheir designs embody the London youth culture with the brand's key ethos being rebellion against the conventional . This has the obvious benefits of not paying shop overheads but it also gives them better control of stock compared to distributing through a retailer.\nThe Corteiz model is to make a product that is desirable, which is achieved in a few ways… Scarcity Marketing One way Corteiz do this is through exclusivity. Exclusivity is a model that's always been prevalent in fashion. It increases brand demand as it's human nature to \"want what you can't have\", which increases revenue .\nTraditionally high-end designers like Louis Vuitton drive exclusivity with premium prices . Higher prices give off the perception a brand is luxurious making them more desirable and improving profits . Increasing prices to this extreme would move Corteiz towards the luxury streetwear demographic which would not mirror their London youth culture design inspiration. This has been chosen on purpose. Studies show that the majority of streetwear consumers will purchase one item a month .\nTherefore having monthly drops increases the likelihood that customers will keep buying from Corteiz. Consumers will be thinking about buying more clothing, then the Corteiz notification will come up. They know if they don't get it now the pieces won't be sold again meaning they are more likely to buy.\n2.3% 11.7% 44.7% 35.3% 6.0% Daily Once a Week Once a Month Once Every 3 Months Once a Year The Problem The streetwear industry is a very saturated market that is dominated by the big brands with illustrious histories.\nFighting with these companies directly will only result in one outcome due to their size and budget differences.\nTherefore to get a foothold in the market, up-and-coming brands have to disrupt the market by doing something different.\nThe Policy Corteiz came from humble beginnings. Clint started off by screen-printing his designs in his room and getting his friends to model them before selling them out the back of his car . Evidently not the business model of an internationally successful company but it allowed the brand to grow organically. Corteiz need to drive hype and desire for their products in order to keep growing the brand, but in a way that means they still grow organically.\nKeeping an authentic message behind the products is essential to keeping customers feeling like they're part of the movement.\nFigure 11: Visual recreation of the Corteiz early days for more recent marketing The Actions No Paid Promotion Corteiz do not pay for any sort of advertisements or sponsors, instead solely relying on their social medias ,creating a very \"if you know, you know\" atmosphere .\nThey post short skits and media pieces on their page.         "content": "[{\"docid\": \"72972\", \"url\": \"https://www.nssmag.com/en/fashion/36100/community-fashion-places-faces-corteiz\", \"score\": 0.5958995819091797, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why communities are so important for brands\\nauthor: Author Sagra de Manueles\\ndate: 2024-03-14\\n---\\nWhy communities are so important for brands\\n\\nBorn in the streetwear world, luxury fashion also wants to recreate them\\n\\nMarch 14th, 2024\\n\\nPossessing its own community is something fundamental for any fashion brand - even though the meaning of the word is often ambiguous. In the best cases, a brand's community forms mostly on its own, albeit with the help and encouragement of the brand itself, as is the case with Diesel, for example; there are many others, especially in the luxury field, where the community and the clientele do not always correspond, leading us to speak more of a \\\"following\\\" than a community, which is more artificially constructed through precise marketing strategies. Either way, a community is needed because it constitutes not so much the audience of a brand, but the people who are under its influence. If a certain collection or brand launches a trend that others follow, think of Miu Miu or Balenciaga in recent years, it is the community that acts as a sounding board for it - what in marketing theory is called \\\"early adopters\\\". Communities play a crucial role in defining a brand identity: the progressive ladies of the 1920s were the community of Chanel, just as CEOs and magnates from around the world represent the community of Brunello Cucinelli or Loro Piana, rock singers are the community of any Hedi Slimane project, and career women with an intellectual side are the community of The Row and Phoebe Philo. There is a clear connection, however, betwee\", \"total_chars\": 5831, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"22731\", \"url\": \"https://www.voguebusiness.com/fashion/corteiz-clint-and-the-future-of-streetwear\", \"score\": 0.573395311832428, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why everyone's talking about Corteiz\\nauthor: Kati Chitrakorn\\ndate: 2022-01-31\\n---\\nTo receive the Vogue Business newsletter, sign up here.\\n\\nOn a weekend in January, groups of young people were spotted climbing fences and running through a car park in Wormwood Scrubs, west London, carrying puffer jackets from brands including The North Face, Stussy, Moncler, Supreme and Arc'teryx. They were following clues to take part in Da Great Bolo Exchange, an event organised by London-based streetwear brand Corteiz. Coordinates were shared on social media along with instructions to bring an authentic branded down jacket in reasonable condition. That made you eligible to receive one of Corteiz's new Bolo jackets. Hundreds of young adults showed up, even though the brand had only 50 jackets to give away.\\n\\nCorteiz (also known as Crtz) was launched in 2017. The founder is known publicly as simply Clint. His pieces — including £30 t-shirts, £120 joggers and £125 cargos — feature a distinctive Alcatraz logo that represents rebellion against convention, considered the core message behind the brand.\\n\\nPieces tend to sell out within minutes. The brand produces a limited run of each product, sold via a private e-commerce site (only those selected are granted access via a password) or at a surprise drop in the physical world. The Instagram account is also private. Resale is discouraged by Corteiz, but difficult to enforce — Bolo jackets are retailing on Depop for £500.\\n\\nClint himself declined to speak with Vogue Business for this story and rarely speaks to press, but it's important not t\", \"total_chars\": 9174, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"69364\", \"url\": \"https://www.gq.com/story/corteiz-brooklyn-denim-exchange-scene-report\", \"score\": 0.5704416632652283, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Inside Corteiz's Frenzied Brooklyn Denim Exchange\\nauthor: Jordan Coley\\ndate: 2024-05-16\\n---\\nOn most Saturday mornings, the post-industrial, post-gentrification blocks of northwest Greenpoint belong to the stroller pushers, the brunchers, the Alo-clad joggers. This particular Saturday is only slightly different. The women in fleeces and leggings toting fiddle leafs from the plant store and the young parents taxiing toddlers to Transmitter Park are there, yes. So too, however, are about 400 anxious 13 to 30 year olds, clamoring for the opportunity to give their pants away.\\n\\nAt about 11 a.m. on a block of West Street just south of Greenpoint Avenue, the air fills with the sound of skidding Citi Bike tires and recently released Air Jordans thudding against the pavement. Suddenly, frantically, a line is forming outside a nondescript warehouse. \\\"DA GREAT DENIM EXCHANGE,\\\" a pop-up event orchestrated by British streetwear label Corteiz, is about to begin—and it's bringing a bit of streetwear hysteria into the neighborhood's millennial equanimity.\\n\\nA day earlier, the brand announced via Instagram that in less than 24 hours it would be doing its second-ever event in New York. According to the post, the first 300 people to arrive and turn in jeans from a select list of brands (\\\"LEVI'S 501s - TRUE RELIGION - CARHARTT JEANS/CARPENTERS - DICKIES - TOMMY HILFIGER - RALPH LAUREN - CALVIN KLEINS - S😜PREME - STUSSY - PALACE - AMIRI\\\") would receive a pair of Corteiz denim in return. Crucially, participants were required to wear their (clean) jeans to the event, hand them in, and wa\", \"total_chars\": 10903, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"93766\", \"url\": \"https://moresneakers.com/blog/detail/corteiz:-the-guerilla-streetwear-brand-that-took-over-london\", \"score\": 0.5700938701629639, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Corteiz: The Guerilla Streetwear Brand That Took Over London\\ndate: 2023-04-12\\n---\\nCorteiz's Unconventional Marketing Tactics\\n\\nIn recent years, it has become rarer to see hordes of shoppers mobbing city streets to buy a limited edition drop from any streetwear label. Many streetwear brands have followed the same playbook - design a seasonal collection, schedule an online release date, and continue selling items via stockists or other retail partners. However, there are brands like Corteiz that have employed unconventional guerilla marketing tactics to capture hype and allure unseen within streetwear in some time.\\n\\nFounded in 2017 by Clint Ogbenna, a British-Nigerian entrepreneur, Corteiz RTW (Rules The World) has become one of the most popular streetwear brands to come out of London since Palace. Within the past five years, the brand's logo of Alcatraz Island has blown up and is now spotted everywhere. The brand's garments have been frequently sighted on UK rap stars such as Central Cee, slowthai, Stormzy, and Dave.\\n\\nCorteiz has gained recognition for its garments among UK rap stars including Central Cee, slowthai, Stormzy, and Dave. In addition, some of the biggest celebrities have given their seal of approval to the brand. Recently, Drake was seen sporting a leather jacket that the brand released this winter, and Pharrell invited the brand's founder, Clint, to a private Friendsgiving dinner held at Selfridges last fall.\\n\\nSurprisingly, Corteiz's social media pages were originally private - for a while, new customers could only learn about the brand's latest relea\", \"total_chars\": 3490, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"37360\", \"url\": \"https://ecoaya.com/blogs/sustainability/community-clothing-brand-communities-sustainable-fashion\", \"score\": 0.5627676248550415, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Community Clothing: Redefining Fashion for a Sustainable Future\\ndate: 2024-10-01\\n---\\nCommunity Clothing:\\n\\nRedefining Fashion for a Sustainable Future\\n\\n.\\n\\nAYA | JANUARY 14, 2025\\n\\nREADING TIME: 7 minutes\\n\\nToday, the fashion industry faces challenges not only from the economic and environmental impacts of fast fashion but also from growing ethical debates that influence consumer purchasing behaviors. As these ethical concerns gain prominence, the concept of community clothing has evolved into something far more than just a trend. Community clothing is now a multifaceted approach to fashion, with each initiative having its own unique impact.\\n\\nIn this article, we explore the diverse landscape of community clothing, with a special focus on those that advocate for sustainability and drive positive change.\\n\\nBrand Communities vs. Community Clothing: Unpacking the Connection\\n\\nA concept closely related to community clothing is brand communities, often mistaken for the same thing. The collective value both terms bring to the table lies in the creation of implicit, discursive, and emotional value for consumers [1]. This overlap can create some confusion. Brand communities aim to strengthen the consumer-brand relationship while fostering a sense of loyalty and understanding between consumers and the community [2,3].\\n\\nThis creates a shared identity and a deeper connection with the brand's vision, turning consumers into \\\"co-creators\\\" of the products [3] or, at the very least, making them feel that their voices and desires influence the brand's projects.\\n\\nSo, what exactly is comm\", \"total_chars\": 15642, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"9472\", \"url\": \"https://www.stu.edu/news/flysupply-stu-fashion-collab-launch/\", \"score\": 0.5577812194824219, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: FlySupply & STU Fashion Collab Launch\\ndate: 2023-10-24\\n---\\nFlySupply & STU Fashion Collab Launch\\n\\nby Walter Villa, Special to STU\\n\\nThis was a match made in heaven – literally.\\n\\nSt. Thomas University, a Catholic institution, and Fly Supply, a clothing line with religious messaging, have made a collaboration blessed by the angels.\\n\\nOn Friday afternoon – accented by a live DJ and tasty food and beverages — students and other guests ventured out to the on-campus Fernandez Family Center lobby to enjoy the launch of Fly Supply's STU line. The sporty line, in an array of bright colors, features messages such as:\\n\\n\\\"GOD GOT MY BACK.\\\"\\n\\n\\\"NEVER SOLD MY SOUL.\\\"\\n\\nAnd …\\n\\n\\\"THE DEVIL IS JEALOUS OF ME.\\\"\\n\\nProfessor Ashlee Rzyczycki, the director of STU's fashion merchandising program, said it was in 2021 that she met the four founders of Fly Supply – Garrett Brown, Rick Maxwell, Kevin Pamphile, and Reginald Bourdeau, all of whom are from Miami.\\n\\nProfessor Rzyczycki quickly decided that working with this hip quartet of designers would be a huge win for St. Thomas University in general, and her students in particular.\\n\\n\\\"They have a great brand,\\\" said Professor Rzyczycki, who was introduced to the Fly Supply guys by STU employee Brandon Vega. \\\"I wanted to incorporate that brand into my classroom.\\\"\\n\\nIn that initial meeting, Professor Rzyczycki said she had an \\\"amazing\\\" two-hour conversation with the Fly Supply guys.\\n\\n\\\"Their brand is super successful,\\\" she said. \\\"I knew this collaboration would really resonate with my students.\\\"\\n\\nFly Supply has previously collaborated with Miami Heat leg\", \"total_chars\": 3707, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"89023\", \"url\": \"https://fashionista.com/2020/08/fashion-brands-celebrity-famous-public-facing-founders\", \"score\": 0.5567072033882141, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Does a Fashion Brand Need a Public-Facing Founder to Survive?\\nauthor: Dhani Mau\\ndate: 2020-08-04\\n---\\nDoes a Fashion Brand Need a Public-Facing Founder to Survive?\\n\\nIn the fashion world, there are a smorgasbord of founders and designers we read and hear about. There's the celebrity designer, which could either mean a celebrity-turned-designer or a designer-turned-celebrity; the socialite designer; the influencer designer (again, that could be an influencer-turned-designer or vice versa); the millennial 'Girlboss' founder; the mythical, legendary designer whose name is everywhere but whose personal life and personality we know little about. With decreasing frequency, it seems, there's also the talented, classically trained, dues-paid, behind-the-scenes designer who wants their work to speak for itself.\\n\\nFashion brands have been harnessing the power of celebrity for over a century. But the \\\"celebrity brand\\\" as we know it really gained traction around the late '90s and early 2000s, thanks to stars like Jay-Z, Sean Combs, Jessica Simpson and more pushing lesser-known names off the sales floor at major retailers like Macy's and upending the entire industry in the process. And there are ways that we still feel this today.\\n\\n\\\"The biggest force in fashion of the early twenty-first century is not designers or manufacturers or retailers. It is, quite simply, fame,\\\" journalist Teri Agins wrote in her 2014 book \\\"Hijacking the Runway,\\\" which chronicled this very phenomenon up to that point. Ove\", \"total_chars\": 2997, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"22731\", \"url\": \"https://www.voguebusiness.com/fashion/corteiz-clint-and-the-future-of-streetwear\", \"score\": 0.6766314506530762, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why everyone's talking about Corteiz\\nauthor: Kati Chitrakorn\\ndate: 2022-01-31\\n---\\nTo receive the Vogue Business newsletter, sign up here.\\n\\nOn a weekend in January, groups of young people were spotted climbing fences and running through a car park in Wormwood Scrubs, west London, carrying puffer jackets from brands including The North Face, Stussy, Moncler, Supreme and Arc'teryx. He had previously started a company called CADE On the Map in 2015, printing tees in his bedroom at the age of 19 before creating Corteiz .2022 Release Breakdown Corteiz release their clothing in 'drops'. This is where brands release a set of items with limited stock with no intention of re-stocking them, so once they're gone, they're gone. The brand has grown meteorically since it's inception, highlighted by musical artists such as Stormzy, Dave and Drake seen sporting Corteiz items . Clint and Corteiz even gained recognition and support from the late designer Virgil Abloh, who transcended the fashion industry and is seen by many as one of the greatest designers in recent history .\\nTheir designs embody the London youth culture with the brand's key ethos being rebellion against the conventional . Cortés is infamous for going against orders and setting off on his own expedition to conquer Mexico in the 1500s . Many streetwear brands have followed the same playbook - design a seasonal collection, schedule an online release date, and continue selling items via stockists or other retail partners. However, there are brands like Corteiz that have employed unconventional guerilla marketing tactics to capture hype and allure unseen within streetwear in some time.\\n\\nFounded in 2017 by Clint Ogbenna, a British-Nigerian entrepreneur, Corteiz RTW (Rules The World) has become one of the most popular streetwear brands to come out of London since Palace. In the best cases, a brand's community forms mostly on its own, albeit with the help and encouragement of the brand itself, as is the case with Diesel, for example; there are many others, especially in the luxury field, where the community and the clientele do not always correspond, leading us to speak more of a \\\"following\\\" than a community, which is more artificially constructed through precise marketing strategies. Either way, a community is needed because it constitutes not so much the audience of a brand, but the people who are under its influence. If a certain collection or brand launches a trend that others follow, think of Miu Miu or Balenciaga in recent years, it is the community that acts as a sounding board for it - what in marketing theory is called \\\"early adopters\\\". Communities play a crucial role in defining a brand identity: the progressive ladies of the 1920s were the community of Chanel, just as CEOs and magnates from around the world represent the community of Brunello Cucinelli or Loro Piana, rock singers are the community of any Hedi Slimane project, and career women with an intellectual side are the community of The Row and Phoebe Philo. Those who pay for Spotify Premium can listen uninterrupted to high-quality recordings and are able to download songs for offline listening.\\n\\nSpotify was founded in 2006 in Stockholm, Sweden, by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. The two wanted to create a legal digital music platform to respond to growing challenge of online music piracy in the early 2000s.\\n\\nEventually convincing record labels to agree to share content in return for an aggregate 20 percent stake, Spotify was launched in 2008.         "content": "{\"docid\": \"77382\", \"url\": \"https://www.businessofapps.com/data/spotify-statistics/\", \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Spotify Revenue and Usage Statistics (2025)\\ndate: 2025-02-25\\n---\\nSpotify is the world's biggest music streaming platform by number of subscribers. Free Spotify access comes with lower sound quality, advertisements and requires an internet connection. Those who pay for Spotify Premium can listen uninterrupted to high-quality recordings and are able to download songs for offline listening.\\n\\nSpotify was founded in 2006 in Stockholm, Sweden, by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. The two wanted to create a legal digital music platform to respond to growing challenge of online music piracy in the early 2000s.\\n\\nEventually convincing record labels to agree to share content in return for an aggregate 20 percent stake, Spotify was launched in 2008. It was an instant success, with a Facebook partnership helping it rise rapidly to prominence. Surviving the transition to mobile, Spotify went public in April 2018, with a market cap of $26.5 billion after the first day of trading.\\n\\nIt has drawn criticism from recording artists, who complain that it pays too little. Claims to democratize the music industry have also been questioned, with the world's biggest four music labels responsible for 87 percent of content available on Spotify.\\n\\nUnfair or not, with the days of physical music long behind us (with the exception of vinyl junkies), Spotify dominates the way we consume music this century. It does have some competition in the field however, its rivals include Apple Music, Amazon and YouTube, alongside smaller and less well funded services.\\n\\nSpotify has branched into podcasts, acquiring some of the leading podcasters and podcast networks, such as the Joe Rogan Experience, The Ringer, and Gimlet Media. It sees this as the next pillar of its streaming service, potentially keeping users locked onto the platform for longer.         "content": "[{\"docid\": \"84696\", \"url\": \"https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2017/03/02/518081927/snapchat-parent-to-begin-trading-on-the-new-york-stock-exchange-thursday\", \"score\": 0.5952717065811157, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Snapchat Parent's Stock Soars By 50 Percent On First Day Of Trading\\nauthor: Doreen McCallister\\ndate: 2017-03-02\\n---\\nSnapchat Parent's Stock Soars By 50 Percent On First Day Of Trading\\n\\nShares of Snap Inc., parent of the popular disappearing-message and camera-centric app Snapchat, rose by more than $8 in the first hours of trading Thursday, as the company watched the $17 price of its initial public offering of 200 million nonvoting shares soar by 50 percent as of mid-day Thursday.\\n\\nThe stock opened above $24 when the new offering began sales shortly after 11 a.m. It then rose above $25 a share, hitting $25.64 by 1:31 p.m.\\n\\nThe initial pricing valued the 5-year-old company, based in Los Angeles, at $24 billion. Earlier projections had expected the range of $14 to $16.\\n\\nLast month, Snap filed paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission to become a publicly traded company.\\n\\nSnap's Snapchat app is best known for disappearing messages and quirky facial filters for jazzing up selfies. It's popular with teenagers and younger millennials.\\n\\nBut despite Snapchat's popularity, user growth has slowed recently.\\n\\nSnapchat started 2017 with 158 million daily active users, most of whom are people in their teens, 20s and early 30s.\\n\\nDoes Snapchat need to go beyond young users to succeed?\\n\\nLaVon Murphy, 45, a photographer in Portland, Ore., told The Associated Press that she uses Snapchat to stay in touch with her 17-year-old son.\\n\\n\\\" 'I don't really understand why he and his friends use the app so extensively, but I am trying to keep up,' she said.\\n\\n\\\" 'It allows me to be\", \"total_chars\": 3113, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"22806\", \"url\": \"https://www.statista.com/statistics/272014/global-social-networks-ranked-by-number-of-users/\", \"score\": 0.53764808177948, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Most used social networks 2025, by number of users\\nauthor: Stacy Jo Dixon; Mar\\ndate: 2025-03-26\\n---\\nMarket leader Facebook was the first social network to surpass one billion registered accounts and currently sits at more than three billion monthly active users. Meta Platforms owns four of the biggest social media platforms, all with more than one billion monthly active users each: Facebook (core platform), WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, and Instagram. In the third quarter of 2023, Facebook reported around four billion monthly core Family product users.\\n\\nThe United States and China account for the most high-profile social platforms\\n\\nMost top ranked social networks with more than 100 million users originated in the United States, but services like Chinese social networks WeChat, QQ or video sharing app Douyin have also garnered mainstream appeal in their respective regions due to local context and content. Douyin's popularity has led to the platform releasing an international version of its network: a little app called TikTok.\\n\\nHow many people use social media?\\n\\nThe leading social networks are usually available in multiple languages and enable users to connect with friends or people across geographical, political, or economic borders. As is understanding other nuances relating to a platform's growth.\\n\\nChoosing which social media network your brand is going to focus on is a very important decision, and one that shouldn't be taken purely on a hunch.\\n\\nSure, a particular social media platform may \\\"feel right\\\" for your brand, but we recommend that you take a bunch of other variables into consideration before making the leap – \\\"relative popularity\\\" and \\\"growth\\\" being two of the most important.\\n\\nTo help your brand with this crucial decision, Dreamgrow maintains this post on the world's biggest 15 social media platforms.
