        "role": "tool",
        "tool_call_id": "call_01_Dl3lqdYpUmfvqji7fw8j4969",
        "content": "{\"docid\": \"86532\", \"url\": \"https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5f02f6f3ff3ad26698daa428/t/659d1f585999ca03a3779b50/1704795995101/Corteiz%2B%281%29.pdf\", \"text\": \"Corteiz Rules the World, also known simply as Corteiz or CRTZ RTW, are a London based streetwear brand. Their items range from jackets and tracksuits down to balaclavas and accessories, for both men and women. Corteiz was established in 2017 by founder Clint Ogbenna, who goes by Clint419 online. He had previously started a company called CADE On the Map in 2015, printing tees in his bedroom at the age of 19 before creating Corteiz .2022 Release Breakdown Corteiz release their clothing in 'drops'. This is where brands release a set of items with limited stock with no intention of re-stocking them, so once they're gone, they're gone. On it's first official drop Corteiz sold just 16 hoodies, fast forward to the present day and every Corteiz drop sells out in minutes making it hard to get a hold of . The brand has grown meteorically since it's inception, highlighted by musical artists such as Stormzy, Dave and Drake seen sporting Corteiz items . Clint and Corteiz even gained recognition and support from the late designer Virgil Abloh, who transcended the fashion industry and is seen by many as one of the greatest designers in recent history .\\nTheir designs embody the London youth culture with the brand's key ethos being rebellion against the conventional . In an old Instagram post the brand said they were inspired by Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés . Cortés is infamous for going against orders and setting off on his own expedition to conquer Mexico in the 1500s . The sense of rebellion is represented best by their Alcatraz logo seen on many of their items. Clint has said via an Instagram story that he looks \\\"at society like one big prison\\\" and \\\"the island represents escaping from the societal constraints that we've grown up with\\\" . This distinctive logo is what helped the brand rise in popularity. The logo itself is actually low quality and has rough edges, giving off a nonchalant, don't-care attitude which adds to the rebellion perception.\\nIt's usually printed across the groin on their trousers and shorts. Many would see this as quite a brash statement but its been very successful with their cargos being some of their most sought after products . They were certainly innovators in this design with lots of brands now copying. Most notoriously BoohooMan who have released tracksuits that are complete imitations.\\nFigure 1: Clint wearing Corteiz Figure 2: Breakdown of items released in 2022, data taken from StockX Figure 3: Corteiz Alcatraz logo The Customers Streetwear is simply defined as fashionable, casual clothing worn by followers of popular culture . The term originated in the 80's, used to describe any sort of counterculture fashion like the hip-hop, surfing or skating scene . Fast forward to the present and these culture have almost become the norm and trendy, causing a surge in popularity for streetwear.\\nThe streetwear market is dominated by young people, with over 60% of consumers being under 25 and largely male. The target market aren't considered the wealthiest, with 70% thought to earn less than $40,000 a year. Most consumers are happy spending roughly $100-$300 per streetwear product . They also tend to live in more urban areas . The Corteiz market is slightly narrower than this. Focusing designs around London youth culture naturally aims there target more at UK consumers. It's thought over 33% of their 250,000 monthly website visits come from the UK .\\nFigure 4: Overview of the average streetwear consumer >25 Majority of consumers are younger than 25 $40000 Most consumers earn less than $40,000 annually URBAN Most customers live in urban areas The Market Streetwear rose into mainstream fashion in the late 2000's and early 10's thanks to the popularity of brands like Supreme and Stussy. The streetwear market has continued to grow year on year and was valued at $173 billion in 2021. It's forecasted to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 1.82% to reach a value of $193 billion by 2027 . Streetwear is now thought to make up around 10% of the entire global footwear and apparel market .\\nThe expected market growth means there is huge business potential for Corteiz. There are lots of competitors which they need to beat, but competition also helps to grow the market. If Corteiz were the only brand in the industry they would be less successful than they are now. Other brands success inadvertently creates more market to go around, benefitting all brands.\\n150 155 160 165 170 175 180 185 190 195 200 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 2027 Global Streetwear Market Worth in Billion U.S. $ Figure 5: Graphic showing past and forecasted streetwear market value Competitors The recent success of streetwear has caught the attention of lots of established brands, creating more competitors.\\nSportwear and luxury brands are working to gain a stake in the streetwear market too . Luxury brands first majorly broke into the market in 2017 when Louis Vuitton collaborated with Supreme . The collab was extremely successful with pieces listed on resale sites for over $25,000 . LV cemented their intentions in streetwear afterwards by appointing Virgil Abloh as the Artistic Director of Menswear . The market is now mixed with original streetwear brands, adopted streetwear brands and luxury streetwear. PwC surveyed 763 apparel brands in streetwear to see how the companies identified themselves .\\nFigure 7: Graphic showing the factors consumers find important in a streetwear brand 36.04% 34.73% 20.18% 9.04% Original SW Brand Adopted Streetwear Luxury Streetwear No Relation Figure 6: Breakdown of how streetwear brands identify themselves Corteiz have really managed to find a sweet spot for their customers.\\nEven since the early days Corteiz's quality has always stood out from its direct competitors and its only improving .\\nThey also offer very reasonable prices, with their t-shirts being around PwC also surveyed consumers to determine which factors they felt where most important in a brand (shown in figure 7). Product quality/design was voted the most influential with 81.4% of people identifying it as important.\\nGiven the masses of brands competing in streetwear now with differing backgrounds, there is a large spread of costs and quality.\\n£30. This is a clever tactic from Corteiz and sets them apart from a lot of the competition. The high quality will ensure customer satisfaction, increasing likelihood of them returning and the low prices create less of a financial barrier. A loyal fanbase are more likely to recommend the brand to fans, increasing the brands reach Highlighted zone is where brands should want to operate for best customer satisfaction Figure 8: Comparing the average T-shirt prices against quality of various competitors Corteiz earns it revenue through the design and distribution of their streetwear products. The sell exclusively from their e-commerce site. This has the obvious benefits of not paying shop overheads but it also gives them better control of stock compared to distributing through a retailer.\\nThe Corteiz model is to make a product that is desirable, which is achieved in a few ways… Scarcity Marketing One way Corteiz do this is through exclusivity. Exclusivity is a model that's always been prevalent in fashion. It increases brand demand as it's human nature to \\\"want what you can't have\\\", which increases revenue .\\nTraditionally high-end designers like Louis Vuitton drive exclusivity with premium prices . Higher prices give off the perception a brand is luxurious making them more desirable and improving profits . Increasing prices to this extreme would move Corteiz towards the luxury streetwear demographic which would not mirror their London youth culture design inspiration. Instead they create exclusivity through scarcity. Corteiz control the number of items produced so the demand is always greater than the supply. This keeps customers wanting. Corteiz take the exclusivity one step further by having their website password protected. This stops just anyone buying clothes. In order to get the password, you need to enter your email on the locked website. Accounts are then selected at random to receive an email announcing a drop and the password a few minutes before it goes live. You then head to the website and type in your password to gain access. Clint also sometimes tweets the password out cryptically too.\\nFigure 9: The two different screens on the website before access Drop System Corteiz release their clothing in 'drops'. This creates hype and makes the items more sought after as they are thought of as limited, and customers will feel like they are missing out on a one time opportunity by not buying. It's a model that has become synonymous with streetwear, made famous by New York based brand Supreme who would release items every Thursday morning . Corteiz do this slightly differently by releasing their drops randomly. They are unveiled on their social medias a few minutes before meaning fans need to be engaged. This makes Corteiz notoriously difficult to purchase .\\nFigure 10: Graph showing how often people buy an item of streetwear Corteiz released around 14 drops in 2022, roughly one a month with extra drops coming on special days i.e. Christmas. This has been chosen on purpose. Studies show that the majority of streetwear consumers will purchase one item a month .\\nTherefore having monthly drops increases the likelihood that customers will keep buying from Corteiz. Consumers will be thinking about buying more clothing, then the Corteiz notification will come up. They know if they don't get it now the pieces won't be sold again meaning they are more likely to buy.\\n2.3% 11.7% 44.7% 35.3% 6.0% Daily Once a Week Once a Month Once Every 3 Months Once a Year The Problem The streetwear industry is a very saturated market that is dominated by the big brands with illustrious histories.\\nFighting with these companies directly will only result in one outcome due to their size and budget differences.\\nTherefore to get a foothold in the market, up-and-coming brands have to disrupt the market by doing something different.\\nThe Policy Corteiz came from humble beginnings. Clint started off by screen-printing his designs in his room and getting his friends to model them before selling them out the back of his car . Evidently not the business model of an internationally successful company but it allowed the brand to grow organically. Corteiz need to drive hype and desire for their products in order to keep growing the brand, but in a way that means they still grow organically.\\nKeeping an authentic message behind the products is essential to keeping customers feeling like they're part of the movement.\\nFigure 11: Visual recreation of the Corteiz early days for more recent marketing The Actions No Paid Promotion Corteiz do not pay for any sort of advertisements or sponsors, instead solely relying on their social medias ,creating a very \\\"if you know, you know\\\" atmosphere .\\nThey post short skits and media pieces on their page. They are always high quality and aren't directly advertising new items, people are just seen wearing them, which doesn't make them feel like adverts. Most clothing brands nowadays pay social media influencers to wear and post about their brand. Corteiz have never done this meaning celebs and artists seen sporting Corteiz are doing so because they believe in the brand's message and have bought the items just like any other customer . Musicians are considered they greatest influence in fashion industry so knowing that your favourite artist like Corteiz will make you want it more. Corteiz have even dropped a special tee in a collab with UK rapper Central Cee which sold out in less than a minute. Clint has said that Central Cee has been supporting Corteiz before their Instagram even had 10k followers and felt it was only right to show some love back Figure 12: Rappers Dave and Central Cee wearing the limited edition Corteiz and Central Cee collab tee Events/Giveaways Corteiz a\", \"offset\": 0, \"total_chars\": 35132, \"truncated\": true, \"next_offset\": 12000}"

        "content": "[{\"docid\": \"69364\", \"url\": \"https://www.gq.com/story/corteiz-brooklyn-denim-exchange-scene-report\", \"score\": 0.5443632006645203, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Inside Corteiz's Frenzied Brooklyn Denim Exchange\\nauthor: Jordan Coley\\ndate: 2024-05-16\\n---\\nOn most Saturday mornings, the post-industrial, post-gentrification blocks of northwest Greenpoint belong to the stroller pushers, the brunchers, the Alo-clad joggers. This particular Saturday is only slightly different. The women in fleeces and leggings toting fiddle leafs from the plant store and the young parents taxiing toddlers to Transmitter Park are there, yes. So too, however, are about 400 anxious 13 to 30 year olds, clamoring for the opportunity to give their pants away.\\n\\nAt about 11 a.m. on a block of West Street just south of Greenpoint Avenue, the air fills with the sound of skidding Citi Bike tires and recently released Air Jordans thudding against the pavement. Suddenly, frantically, a line is forming outside a nondescript warehouse. \\\"DA GREAT DENIM EXCHANGE,\\\" a pop-up event orchestrated by British streetwear label Corteiz, is about to begin—and it's bringing a bit of streetwear hysteria into the neighborhood's millennial equanimity.\\n\\nA day earlier, the brand announced via Instagram that in less than 24 hours it would be doing its second-ever event in New York. According to the post, the first 300 people to arrive and turn in jeans from a select list of brands (\\\"LEVI'S 501s - TRUE RELIGION - CARHARTT JEANS/CARPENTERS - DICKIES - TOMMY HILFIGER - RALPH LAUREN - CALVIN KLEINS - S😜PREME - STUSSY - PALACE - AMIRI\\\") would receive a pair of Corteiz denim in return. There are many steps marketers have to take in order to pull off attention-grabbing influencer activations, and one of the first is deciding what format a campaign will take and where it will appear.\\n\\nIf you're planning an influencer marketing campaign of your own, you already know the bar is high! To give you a sense of the possibilities, we rounded up some examples of the best influencer marketing campaigns that have come across our phone and laptop screens in recent years. Great for driving brand awareness, these campaigns capitalize on an influencer's popularity and social media following, no matter how big or small.\\n\\nInfluencers with smaller followings, such as micro-influencers and nano-influencers, help marketers\", \"total_chars\": 20073, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"29644\", \"url\": \"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/himanshu-chandnani-504ba9144_influencermarketing-marketing-influencer-activity-7200107552678817792-b_xB\", \"score\": 0.5409941673278809, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Himanshu Chandnani's Post\\nauthor: 7\\ndate: 2025-01-01\\n---\\nHow this brand chose Bhuvan Bam as their first ambassador! Imagine you watch someone daily on your phone, making you laugh and sharing their daily vlogs with you, and suddenly they are now a brand ambassador for the popular clothing brand 'Beyoung'. – What will the impact be? – Will it affect the brand's visibility? – What about the annual turnover? You heard it right; in October 2023, Bhuvan Bam became the first brand ambassador of 'Be Young', and the team responded… \\\"Both Be Young and Bhuvan Bam understand the value of hard work and determination, as we've each journeyed from nothing to a family of millions. Together, we're on a mission to transform the fashion landscape in India.         "content": "{\"docid\": \"7940\", \"url\": \"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Francis\", \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Ben Francis - Wikipedia\\ndate: 2020-08-14\\n---\\nname: Ben Francis\\nhonorific_suffix: GBR 100% MBE\\nbirth_name: Benjamin David Francis\\nbirth_date: 04 06 1992\\nbirth_place: West Midlands, England\\neducation: South Bromsgrove High School\\nalma_mater: Aston University (dropped out)\\nknown for: Co-founder, CEO and majority owner of Gymshark\\nspouse: Robin Gallant (m. 2021)\\nchildren: 2\\nwebsite: benfrancis.com\\n\\nBenjamin David Francis (born 4 June 1992) is a British businessman. He is the co-founder, CEO and majority owner of Gymshark, a fitness apparel and accessories company founded in 2012.\\n\\nWith a stake of over 70% in Gymshark which is currently valued by investors at $1.45 billion, Francis had a net worth of $1.3 billion as of April 2023. In April 2023, he made his debut on Forbes' annual The World's Billionaires list as the 2,259th richest person in the world.\\n\\nEarly life\\n\\nBenjamin David Francis was born in the West Midlands, England in 1992 and grew up in Bromsgrove, Worcestershire. He attended South Bromsgrove High School. He first became interested in computing after studying IT at school. His first business was an online company that sold car number plates. Francis started going to the gym as a teenager. He later said \\\"the structure, consistency and work ethic I found in the gym I realised, could be applied to different areas of my life and it would work.\\\" In 2010, he enrolled at Aston University for international business and management wherein he had \\\"a strong foundation on which to build a business.\\\" He dropped out in 2012.\\n\\nCareer\\n\\nBefore launching Gymshark, Francis developed two fitness applications, Fat Loss Abs Guide and . While at university between 2010 and 2013, he worked for Pizza Hut as a delivery boy earning £5 an hour. He left six months after launching Gymshark.\\n\\nGymshark\\n\\nIn 2012, at 19, he launched Gymshark in his parents' garage with school friend Lewis Morgan. The website initially sold fitness supplements. Unable to afford to buy stock or secure distribution deals with supplement suppliers, he began dropshipping supplies from other vendors and it took him six weeks to make his first sale. In 2013, branching out from supplements, Francis began designing and selling fitness apparel on Gymshark's website. He began manufacturing the products from his parents' garage in Bromsgrove, using a sewing machine and screen printer he bought with £1,000 of savings. He learned how to sew from his grandmother.\\n\\nIn 2013, he exhibited Gymshark's products at the BodyPower fitness trade show in Birmingham. After the trade show ended, a tracksuit went viral on Facebook, generating £30,000 in sales within 30 minutes. Francis later left university and quit his job at Pizza Hut to focus on the company full-time. As a start-up, Francis marketed the brand through partnering with social media influencers, including body builders Nikki Blackketter and Lex Griffin. Gymshark was one of the first brands to make extensive use of social media influencers.\\n\\nIn 2015, Francis stepped down as CEO of the company to become chief marketing officer, chief brand officer and chief product officer. At the time, he said the move would allow the company \\\"to grow even more quickly\\\" and give him time to \\\"work on my weaknesses and become a more rounded businessperson\\\". In 2018, Gymshark opened a new £5 million headquarters in Solihull, West Midlands. In 2019, Gymshark opened its own branded gym and innovation hub. Since 2016, Gymshark has been listed on The Sunday Times Fast Track of fast-growing private companies. The company currently sells products in 131 countries.\\n\\nIn August 2020, Gymshark sold a 21% stake to US private equity firm General Atlantic in a deal which valued the company in excess of £1 billion. Francis currently owns more than 70% of the company, which is worth £700 million. In August 2021, he returned to the role of the company's CEO.\\n\\nIn 2018, Francis was included on the Forbes 30 Under 30 list. In 2019, Francis served on the UK Government's Business Council for Entrepreneurs. In 2020, Francis was awarded the EY UK Entrepreneur of the Year Award. Francis was appointed Member of the Order of the British Empire (MBE) in the 2023 New Year Honours for services to the business sector.\\n\\nPersonal life\\n\\nFrancis is a car and motorcycle enthusiast, and a season ticket holder at Aston Villa. He and his girlfriend Robin Gallant became engaged in April 2021, and married on 9 September 2021. On 8 September 2022, Francis announced that they were expecting twins. Their twin sons were born on 24 December 2022.         "content": "{\"docid\": \"19241\", \"url\": \"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandora_(service)\", \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Pandora (service) - Wikipedia\\ndate: 2005-11-28\\n---\\nname: Pandora\\nlogo: Pandora wordmark.svg\\ntype: Music streaming service\\nlocation: Oakland, California, U.S.\\nlocations: 7\\nfounder: Will GlaserJon KraftTim Westergren\\nservices: Internet radio\\nprogramming_language: Java\\nadvertising: Banner ads, video ads, audio ads\\nregistration: Optional (required to save stations)\\ncompany_type: Subsidiary\\nlanguage: English\\nnative_clients: Universal Windows App, iOS, Android\\nfoundation: 2000 (as Savage Beast Technologies)Oakland, California, U.S.\\narea_served: United States\\nnum_employees: 1, 938 (2019)Pandora Media LLC Company Profile Bloomberg Markets July 21, 2020\\nparent: Sirius XM (2019–present)\\nsubsidiaries: Rdio (as of December 22, 2015), Next Big Sound (as of November 1, 2021) Adswizz (as of May 29, 2018) Stitcher (as of August 29, 2023)\\nnum_users: 55.9 million active (2021), Pandora ended Q1 2021 with 55.9m monthly active listeners - Music Ally April 29, 2021 6.4 million subscribers (2021) Pandora ended Q1 2021 with 55.9m monthly active listeners - Music Ally April 29, 2021\\ncurrent_status: Active\\nfootnotes: 2019 Form 10-K Annual Report SiriusXM Holdings July 21, 2020\\n\\nPandora is a subscription-based music streaming service owned by the broadcasting corporation Sirius XM that is based in Oakland, California in the United States. The service carries a focus on recommendations based on the \\\"Music Genome Project\\\", which is a means of classifying individual songs by musical traits such as genres and shared instrumentation. The service originally launched in the consumer market as an internet radio service that would generate personalized channels based on these traits as well as specific tracks liked by the user; this service is available in an advertising-supported tier and additionally a subscription-based version. In 2017, the service launched Pandora Premium, which is an on-demand version of the service more in line with contemporary competitors.\\n\\nThe company was founded in 2000 as Savage Beast Technologies, and initially conceived as a business-to-business company licensing the Music Genome Project to retailers as a recommendation platform. In 2005, the company shifted its focus to the consumer market by launching Pandora as an internet radio product. Pandora is a freemium service; basic features are free with advertisements or limitations, while additional features, such as improved streaming quality, music downloads and offline channels are offered via paid subscriptions.\\n\\nIn February 2019, Sirius XM acquired Pandora for $3.5 billion in stock. In 2021, Pandora had about 55.9 million active monthly users, and 6.4 million subscribers. , Pandora reportedly had fewer than 50 million active users. As of 2023, there were 46 million users.\\n\\nHistory\\n\\nEarly history\\n\\nIn 2000, Will Glaser, Jon Kraft, and Tim Westergren founded the company as Savage Beast Technologies. Will Glaser had conceptualized the concept of classifying music by various traits and attributes—an effort that he would later name the \\\"Music Genome Project\\\". The company was originally pitched as an e-commerce service that would use Glaser's associated algorithm as a recommendation engine, but this idea was scrapped after the Dot-com bubble hit its peak in March 2000. Afterwards, the company pursued licensing the technology to other retailers, such as AOL Music and Best Buy (who used it for in-store kiosks as a trial).\\n\\nThe company faced increasing debt, and ran through its initial $2 million in funding by 2001. Glaser, Kraft, and Westergren then convinced Savage Beast's 50 employees to work for two years without pay, prompting a lawsuit by former employees in 2003 due to deferred salaries being illegal under California law. After settling the suit, just a few employees were laid off. In 2004, based on the success of the Best Buy pilot, Walden Venture Capital led an $8 million round of funding, and hired Joe Kennedy—formerly of automaker Saturn—as its new CEO. After agreements with Best Buy and Borders lapsed, the company began to shift its attention to the consumer market, resulting in the development of Pandora as an internet radio service using the Music Genome Project as a personalization system.\\n\\nAfter a beta period, Pandora officially launched in August 2005. Upon its launch, it was a subscription-based service, but added a free, ad-supported version in November after Westergren realized users were abusing its 10-hour free trial by making new e-mail addresses. Advertising could also be targeted based on the current song.\\n\\nGrowth\\n\\nIn 2011, Pandora went public via an initial public offering on the New York Stock Exchange. At the time, Pandora had 800,000 tracks from 80,000 artists in its library and 80 million users. As of end of mid-year 2018, Pandora had 71.4 million active users.\\n\\nOn March 7, 2013, Pandora chairman and chief executive officer Joseph J. Kennedy announced that he would leave the company after nine years.\\n\\nIn April 2013, Pandora announced that its radio streaming service had 200 million users, including 70 million monthly active users. By December 2013, Pandora accounted for 70% of all internet radio listening in the United States.\\n\\nOn September 1, 2013, Pandora removed a 40-hour-per-month limitation for free mobile listening. As of October 2014, less than 5 percent of active listeners were paying subscribers.\\n\\nBy November 2014, Pandora had approximately doubled its library size, topping 1.5 million songs.\\n\\nOn September 15, 2016, Pandora launched \\\"Pandora Plus\\\", a new $4.99 subscription service to compete with other streaming services.\\n\\nIn early 2017, Pandora revealed that 56 million of its 81 million active users subscribed to the Today's Country station and that country music had accounted for more than 1.7 billion listening hours on the platform in 2016.\\n\\nOn July 31, 2017, Pandora discontinued services in Australia and New Zealand, citing a need to focus solely on the U.S. market.\\n\\nIn September 2017, Roger Lync\", \"offset\": 0, \"total_chars\": 25508, \"truncated\": true, \"next_offset\": 6000}"

        "content": "[{\"docid\": \"69364\", \"url\": \"https://www.gq.com/story/corteiz-brooklyn-denim-exchange-scene-report\", \"score\": 0.561578094959259, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Inside Corteiz's Frenzied Brooklyn Denim Exchange\\nauthor: Jordan Coley\\ndate: 2024-05-16\\n---\\nOn most Saturday mornings, the post-industrial, post-gentrification blocks of northwest Greenpoint belong to the stroller pushers, the brunchers, the Alo-clad joggers. This particular Saturday is only slightly different. The women in fleeces and leggings toting fiddle leafs from the plant store and the young parents taxiing toddlers to Transmitter Park are there, yes. So too, however, are about 400 anxious 13 to 30 year olds, clamoring for the opportunity to give their pants away.\\n\\nAt about 11 a.m. on a block of West Street just south of Greenpoint Avenue, the air fills with the sound of skidding Citi Bike tires and recently released Air Jordans thudding against the pavement. Suddenly, frantically, a line is forming outside a nondescript warehouse. \\\"DA GREAT DENIM EXCHANGE,\\\" a pop-up event orchestrated by British streetwear label Corteiz, is about to begin—and it's bringing a bit of streetwear hysteria into the neighborhood's millennial equanimity.\\n\\nA day earlier, the brand announced via Instagram that in less than 24 hours it would be doing its second-ever event in New York. According to the post, the first 300 people to arrive and turn in jeans from a select list of brands (\\\"LEVI'S 501s - TRUE RELIGION - CARHARTT JEANS/CARPENTERS - DICKIES - TOMMY HILFIGER - RALPH LAUREN - CALVIN KLEINS - S😜PREME - STUSSY - PALACE - AMIRI\\\") would receive a pair of Corteiz denim in return. Crucially, participants were required to wear their (clean) jeans to the event, hand them in, and wa\", \"total_chars\": 10903, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"24591\", \"url\": \"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corteiz\", \"score\": 0.5161648392677307, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Corteiz - Wikipedia\\ndate: 2024-04-20\\n---\\nname: Corteiz\\ncurrentowner: Clint 419\\ncountry: United Kingdom\\ntagline: Rules The World\\norigin: United Kingdom\\nproducttype: Apparel\\n\\nCorteiz Rules The World (CRTZ) is a London-based streetwear brand founded in 2017 by British-Nigerian entrepreneur Clint Ogbenna, professionally known as Clint 419. The brand's logo features Alcatraz, the former prison island. The clothes also feature the tagline \\\"Rules The World\\\".\\n\\nHistory\\n\\nCorteiz was founded in 2017. It first launched a limited collection of screen-printed t-shirts and crewnecks featuring the Alcatraz logo. The logo is symbolic of the brand's main message, which is rebellion against convention. The brand has since then expanded its product offering including tracksuits, shoes and bags. Corteiz has a Instagram account and a website that is only accessible using a password.\\n\\nCorteiz is known for its use of guerilla marketing strategies. In 2021, Corteiz launched their tshirt in Soho. Customers would exchange their metro tickets for the limited Corteiz Tshirt.\\n\\nIn 2022, the brand launched 'Da Great Bolo Exchange'. The brand's founder Clint via Twitter (now X) invited Corteiz customers to swap their jackets from high-end brands such as The North Face, Moncler, Supreme, Canada Goose, Stüssy, Arc'teryx and Palace, for the new Corteiz Bolo jacket. The jackets collected were donated to the homeless.\\n\\nIn 2022, Corteiz held the '99p Market Stall' pop-up to sell their new cargos for 99 pence. The requirement was that customers show up with exactly 99p and no change would be given. Ove\", \"total_chars\": 2997, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"86532\", \"url\": \"https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5f02f6f3ff3ad26698daa428/t/659d1f585999ca03a3779b50/1704795995101/Corteiz%2B%281%29.pdf\", \"score\": 0.49075639247894287, \"text\": \"Corteiz Rules the World, also known simply as Corteiz or CRTZ RTW, are a London based streetwear brand. He had previously started a company called CADE On the Map in 2015, printing tees in his bedroom at the age of 19 before creating Corteiz .2022 Release Breakdown Corteiz release their clothing in 'drops'. This is where brands release a set of items with limited stock with no intention of re-stocking them, so once they're gone, they're gone. On it's first official drop Corteiz sold just 16 hoodies, fast forward to the present day and every Corteiz drop sells out in minutes making it hard to get a hold of . The brand has grown meteorically since it's inception, highlighted by musical artists such as Stormzy, Dave and Drake seen sporting Corteiz items . Clint and Corteiz even gained recognition and support from the late designer Virgil Abloh, who transcended the fashion industry and is seen by many as one of the greatest designers in recent history .\\nTheir designs embody the London youth culture with the brand's key ethos being rebellion against the conventional . Cortés is infamous for going against orders and setting off on his own expedition to conquer Mexico in the 1500s . The sense of rebellion is represented best by their Alcatraz logo seen on many of their items. Clint has said via\", \"total_chars\": 35132, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"22731\", \"url\": \"https://www.voguebusiness.com/fashion/corteiz-clint-and-the-future-of-streetwear\", \"score\": 0.4651142358779907, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why everyone's talking about Corteiz\\nauthor: Kati Chitrakorn\\ndate: 2022-01-31\\n---\\nTo receive the Vogue Business newsletter, sign up here.\\n\\nOn a weekend in January, groups of young people were spotted climbing fences and running through a car park in Wormwood Scrubs, west London, carrying puffer jackets from brands including The North Face, Stussy, Moncler, Supreme and Arc'teryx. They were following clues to take part in Da Great Bolo Exchange, an event organised by London-based streetwear brand Corteiz. Coordinates were shared on social media along with instructions to bring an authentic branded down jacket in reasonable condition. That made you eligible to receive one of Corteiz's new Bolo jackets. Hundreds of young adults showed up, even though the brand had only 50 jackets to give away.\\n\\nCorteiz (also known as Crtz) was launched in 2017. The founder is known publicly as simply Clint. His pieces — including £30 t-shirts, £120 joggers and £125 cargos — feature a distinctive Alcatraz logo that represents rebellion against convention, considered the core message behind the brand.\\n\\nPieces tend to sell out within minutes. The brand produces a limited run of each product, sold via a private e-commerce site (only those selected are granted access via a password) or at a surprise drop in the physical world. The Instagram account is also private. Earlier projections had expected the range of $14 to $16.\\n\\nLast month, Snap filed paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission to become a publicly traded company.\\n\\nSnap's Snapchat app is best known for disappearing messages and quirky facial filters for jazzing up selfies. It's popular with teenagers and younger millennials.\\n\\nBut despite Snapchat's popularity, user growth has slowed recently.\\n\\nSnapchat started 2017 with 158 million daily active users, most of whom are people in their teens, 20s and early 30s.\\n\\nDoes Snapchat need to go beyond young users to succeed?\\n\\nLaVon Murphy, 45, a photographer in Portland, Ore., told The Associated Press that she uses Snapchat to stay in touch with her 17-year-old son.\\n\\n\\\" 'I don't really understand why he and his friends use the app so extensively, but I am trying to keep up,' she said.\\n\\n\\\" \"---\\ntitle: Number of ChatGPT Users (March 2025)\\nauthor: Fabio Duarte\\ndate: 2025-06-05\\n---\\nNumber of ChatGPT Users (March 2025)\\n\\nOpenAI's ChatGPT took off in record-breaking TheFacebook, as it was then known, was originally intended to serve a digitised version of the 'face books' held by Harvard's various colleges, which were paper directories containing images and personal information about students.\\n\\nInitially limited to Harvard, Facebook expanded to include students at other elite US universities, before branching out to all universities and high schools in the US and Canada. In 2006, it was finally decided to open the site up to the general public.\\n\\nTurn installs into active and engaged customers\\n\\nGrow in-app revenue and build user loyalty with custom retargeting and churn prediction campaigns from Adikteev.\\n\\nGet startedOver the years Facebook has expanded to include multimedia content and sharing content initially posted by others on Facebook or elsewhere. All stuff that seems rudimentary to us now, but at the time were pioneering innovations from Facebook and other members of that first post-MySpace wave of social networks.\\n\\nPrivate message functionality eventually became standalone app, Facebook Messenger, though is still part of the desktop site. Headlines\\n\\nAs we've seen in our on-going series of Digital Statshot reports, mobile increasingly dominates the digital world, and we're confident that 'ubiquitous connectivity' will gather even Messenger achieving the top social media ranking spots in some of the world's biggest economies, it's clear that much of our digital behaviour is now converging around mobile devices.\\n\\nBased on the trends within this data, we expect that mobile will help to push internet penetration beyond 50% of the world's population during mid to late 2016.\\n\\nBefore that, though, we expect to see         "content": "[{\"docid\": \"93766\", \"url\": \"https://moresneakers.com/blog/detail/corteiz:-the-guerilla-streetwear-brand-that-took-over-london\", \"score\": 0.5969376564025879, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Corteiz: The Guerilla Streetwear Brand That Took Over London\\ndate: 2023-04-12\\n---\\nCorteiz's Unconventional Marketing Tactics\\n\\nIn recent years, it has become rarer to see hordes of shoppers mobbing city streets to buy a limited edition drop from any streetwear label. Many streetwear brands have followed the same playbook - design a seasonal collection, schedule an online release date, and continue selling items via stockists or other retail partners. However, there are brands like Corteiz that have employed unconventional guerilla marketing tactics to capture hype and allure unseen within streetwear in some time.\\n\\nFounded in 2017 by Clint Ogbenna, a British-Nigerian entrepreneur, Corteiz RTW (Rules The World) has become one of the most popular streetwear brands to come out of London since Palace. Within the past five years, the brand's logo of Alcatraz Island has blown up and is now spotted everywhere. The brand's garments have been frequently sighted on UK rap stars such as Central Cee, slowthai, Stormzy, and Dave.\\n\\nCorteiz has gained recognition for its garments among UK rap stars including Central Cee, slowthai, Stormzy, and Dave. In addition, some of the biggest celebrities have given their seal of approval to the brand. Recently, Drake was seen sporting a leather jacket that the brand released this winter, and Pharrell invited the brand's founder, Clint, to a private Friendsgiving dinner held at Selfridges last fall.\\n\\nSurprisingly, Corteiz's social media pages were originally private - for a while, new customers could only learn about the brand's latest relea\", \"total_chars\": 3490, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"22731\", \"url\": \"https://www.voguebusiness.com/fashion/corteiz-clint-and-the-future-of-streetwear\", \"score\": 0.5743364095687866, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why everyone's talking about Corteiz\\nauthor: Kati Chitrakorn\\ndate: 2022-01-31\\n---\\nTo receive the Vogue Business newsletter, sign up here.\\n\\nOn a weekend in January, groups of young people were spotted climbing fences and running through a car park in Wormwood Scrubs, west London, carrying puffer jackets from brands including The North Face, Stussy, Moncler, Supreme and Arc'teryx. They were following clues to take part in Da Great Bolo Exchange, an event organised by London-based streetwear brand Corteiz. Coordinates were shared on social media along with instructions to bring an authentic branded down jacket in reasonable condition. That made you eligible to receive one of Corteiz's new Bolo jackets. Hundreds of young adults showed up, even though the brand had only 50 jackets to give away.\\n\\nCorteiz (also known as Crtz) was launched in 2017. The founder is known publicly as simply Clint. His pieces — including £30 t-shirts, £120 joggers and £125 cargos — feature a distinctive Alcatraz logo that represents rebellion against convention, considered the core message behind the brand.\\n\\nPieces tend to sell out within minutes. The brand produces a limited run of each product, sold via a private e-commerce site (only those selected are granted access via a password) or at a surprise drop in the physical world. The Instagram account is also private. Resale is discouraged by Corteiz, but difficult to enforce — Bolo jackets are retailing on Depop for £500.\\n\\nClint himself declined to speak with Vogue Business for this story and rarely speaks to press, but it's important not t\", \"total_chars\": 9174, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"86532\", \"url\": \"https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5f02f6f3ff3ad26698daa428/t/659d1f585999ca03a3779b50/1704795995101/Corteiz%2B%281%29.pdf\", \"score\": 0.5692979097366333, \"text\": \"Corteiz Rules the World, also known simply as Corteiz or CRTZ RTW, are a London based streetwear brand. Their items range from jackets and tracksuits down to balaclavas and accessories, for both men and women. Corteiz was established in 2017 by founder Clint Ogbenna, who goes by Clint419 online. In the best cases, a brand's community forms mostly on its own, albeit with the help and encouragement of the brand itself, as is the case with Diesel, for example; there are many others, especially in the luxury field, where the community and the clientele do not always correspond, leading us to speak more of a \\\"following\\\" than a community, which is more artificially constructed through precise marketing strategies. Either way, a community is needed because it constitutes not so much the audience of a brand, but the people who are under its influence. If a certain collection or brand launches a trend that others follow, think of Miu Miu or Balenciaga in recent years, it is the community that acts as a sounding board for it - what in marketing theory is called \\\"early adopters\\\".     "url": "https://www.voguebusiness.com/fashion/corteiz-clint-and-the-future-of-streetwear",
    "text": "---\ntitle: Why everyone's talking about Corteiz\nauthor: Kati Chitrakorn\ndate: 2022-01-31\n---\nTo receive the Vogue Business newsletter, sign up here.\n\nOn a weekend in January, groups of young people were spotted climbing fences and running through a car park in Wormwood Scrubs, west London, carrying puffer jackets from brands including The North Face, Stussy, Moncler, Supreme and Arc'teryx. They were following clues to take part in Da Great Bolo Exchange, an event organised by London-based streetwear brand Corteiz. Coordinates were shared on social media along with instructions to bring an authentic branded down jacket in reasonable condition. That made you eligible to receive one of Corteiz's new Bolo jackets. Hundreds of young adults showed up, even though the brand had only 50 jackets to give away.\n\nCorteiz (also known as Crtz) was launched in 2017. The founder is known publicly as simply Clint. His pieces — including £30 t-shirts, £120 joggers and £125 cargos — feature a distinctive Alcatraz logo that represents rebellion against convention, considered the core message behind the brand.\n\nPieces tend to sell out within minutes. The brand produces a limited run of each product, sold via a private e-commerce site (only those selected are granted access via a password) or at a surprise drop in the physical world. The Instagram account is also private. Resale is discouraged by Corteiz, but difficult to enforce — Bolo jackets are retailing on Depop for £500.\n\nClint himself declined to speak with Vogue Business for this story and rarely speaks to press, but it's important not to overlook how this brand, and its hugely engaged community, is evolving. Corteiz is a new kind of modern streetwear brand that is keen to set itself apart from other players in a global streetwear industry worth $185 billion, according to PWC, with an egalitarian attitude and tight-knit community drawn to the anti-establishment ethos. A January tweet to tease the event read: \"All the people who've had their norfy for 3 years+ & its been ran tru, battered and bruised. Tomorrow is your time to redeem it for something that will keep you warmer, satisfied & drippier. 50 Bolo's only. Safe.\"\n\nCorteiz is tapping into a sector that has lost touch with its origins in a drive to make money, according to Laura Leeb, a director at PWC's strategy consulting arm Strategy& and author of the company's Streetwear: The New Exclusivity report. Counter-cultural authenticity has been replaced by the commercial imperatives of a multi-billion dollar retail market for the under-25s, she says.\n\nThe rise of secondhand channels like StockX, Grailed and Goat has also nurtured a $36 billion resale industry where consumers can make money from selling rare, limited-edition sneakers and other collectible pieces. The market is expected to more than double to $77 billion in the next five years, according to 2021 data from Thredup. Streetwear has become mass, says Leeb. \"Many luxury brands are redefining themselves as streetwear brands – and existing players like Supreme have gotten massive due to acquisitions.\"\n\nThis is not Clint's first brand. A predecessor to Corteiz was Cade, which he founded in 2015 with his friend Ade Sanusi at the age of 19. Both were part of Apex, a London-based collective of creative teenagers who bonded over self expression and personal style while maintaining an IDGAF attitude. It's unclear when the brand stopped operating.\n\nCorteiz has over 190,000 followers on Instagram and more than 32,700 on Twitter. In January 2022, it was one of the most searched-for brands in the UK on Depop, with its joggers particularly popular. The brand's fans included the late Virgil Abloh, founder of streetwear brand Off-White and artistic director of Louis Vuitton menswear, who wore Corteiz's \"Rules The World\" socks to the Met Gala in September 2021, as well as influential British music artists such as Slowthai, Jorja Smith, KwolleM and Central Cee.\n\nConnecting with fans\n\nThe Corteiz fandom is spectacular, observers say. \"I haven't seen that in fashion in a long time,\" says Cody Eastmond, who has worked on digital marketing campaigns at creative agency Science Magic with brands such as Glossier and Versace. \"Supreme had some of that — where people would sit outside and wait to get into the store. But, many streetwear brands have matured and lost that locality.\"\n\nDarnell Ferguson documents Corteiz's drops on his YouTube account Darnell Vlogs, which has 58,000 subscribers, and Instagram account @dvrnsz with over 19,000 followers. \"I've seen the hype… People were missing work to come and swap their jackets, without the guarantee of even getting a coat,\" he says. \"I haven't seen another brand do something quite like what Corteiz is doing.\"\n\nAuthenticity is core to the brand message of Corteiz, which is marketed only through social media, standing out in contrast to the heavy marketing spend of mainstream streetwear brands. \"Corteiz doesn't gift people or pay for promotions, so the celebrities you see rocking it have believed in it,\" says Sandy Kaur, the London-based entrepreneur behind the platform and podcast Her Story In Sneakers, who first discovered Corteiz through the sneaker community in 2019. \"The garms are high quality but they aren't gentrified. The company is Black-owned and very much stands for London culture. It's an 'if-you-know-you-know' brand when you wear it out and about.\"\n\nWhy does this matter? \"Buying from Crtz allows people to feel like they're part of a community,\" says Kaur. \"I mean, Central Cee wore a full Crtz fit to the Louis Vuitton fashion show and didn't look out of place. That has to count for something, right?\"\n\nThe feeling of connectivity matters intensely to many younger consumers who are still exploring and developing their personalities, says Pavel Dler, founder and chief executive of youth media company Culted. \"There's a gap in the market for brands that make you feel like you belong. Brands often struggle to authentically connect with young fashion and streetwear enthusiasts because they fail to be transparent about their values and contribution towards communities that they're trying to reach,\" he explains. \"Corteiz does all of these things without even trying. It's just clothes, made by the community for the community, in a way that brings them together.\"\n\nStreetwear's assimilation into the mainstream\n\nAs traditional marketing loses traction with younger consumers, some fashion brands have experimented with streetwear-style drops to create hype. Specialist streetwear designers are being courted. In January, Swiss luxury brand Bally named 29-year-old Rhuigi Villaseñor, founder of streetwear brand Rhude, as its new creative director. In a series of appointments in 2021, LVMH made A Bathing Ape founder Nigo creative director of Kenzo; Gap struck a 10-year-deal for a Yeezy partnership with Kanye West; and J Crew hired as its new creative director Brendon Babenzien, former creative director of Supreme and founder of streetwear label Noah.\n\nThe challenge for the streetwear industry is to stay true to its original roots, says Culted's Dler. \"In recent years it has been commodified and glamourised. It's been boxed and labelled as one thing, but it's bigger and more fluid than that.\"\n\nCorteiz returns to streetwear's beginnings, observes Felix Katt, engagement manager at PWC's Strategy&. \"The underlying theme here is accessibility and non-conformity. It's not about whether you're wealthy and can afford it, but rather it's about being part of the community and therefore being in the know,\" he says.\n\nYounger fans are receptive, Eastmond observes. \"They're used to this behaviour. There are Discord and Reddit forums where people share information on how to get access. For brands, it's about knowing your audience and how to communicate with them.\"\n\nSocial responsibility initiatives appeal to this community. The January down jacket swap event had a surprising charitable twist. Three days later, Clint revealed that all the jackets were donated to St Laurence's Larder, a London-based organisation that provides meals for the homeless and those in need. \"I've recently seen more environmental, social and governance (ESG) campaigns,\" says Strategy&'s Katt. \"That makes sense because streetwear is about being in touch with a brand that aligns with your personal values. It's a new undercurrent in streetwear that I personally didn't see two or three years ago.\"\n\nCould Corteiz lead a return to a more authentic kind of streetwear? \"Corporations and fashion houses have profited from a culture that was never really theirs, and the only place streetwear can really head next is returning to where it originated,\" says entrepreneur Kaur. \"Corteiz is hot right now due to the noise it made, but it will survive beyond being a trend because its core base never relied on the support of the masses. Corteiz isn't hype — it's London.\"\n\nClarification: Removes full name of Clint per request of the founder due to safety concerns. (31 January 2022)\n\nComments, questions or feedback? Email us at feedback@voguebusiness.com.\n\nWhat the Supreme VF deal means for streetwear",

    "text": "---\ntitle: Corteiz: The Guerilla Streetwear Brand That Took Over London\ndate: 2023-04-12\n---\nCorteiz's Unconventional Marketing Tactics\n\nIn recent years, it has become rarer to see hordes of shoppers mobbing city streets to buy a limited edition drop from any streetwear label. Many streetwear brands have followed the same playbook - design a seasonal collection, schedule an online release date, and continue selling items via stockists or other retail partners. However, there are brands like Corteiz that have employed unconventional guerilla marketing tactics to capture hype and allure unseen within streetwear in some time.\n\nFounded in 2017 by Clint Ogbenna, a British-Nigerian entrepreneur, Corteiz RTW (Rules The World) has become one of the most popular streetwear brands to come out of London since Palace. Within the past five years, the brand's logo of Alcatraz Island has blown up and is now spotted everywhere. The brand's garments have been frequently sighted on UK rap stars such as Central Cee, slowthai, Stormzy, and Dave.\n\nCorteiz has gained recognition for its garments among UK rap stars including Central Cee, slowthai, Stormzy, and Dave. In addition, some of the biggest celebrities have given their seal of approval to the brand. Recently, Drake was seen sporting a leather jacket that the brand released this winter, and Pharrell invited the brand's founder, Clint, to a private Friendsgiving dinner held at Selfridges last fall.\n\nSurprisingly, Corteiz's social media pages were originally private - for a while, new customers could only learn about the brand's latest releases if their \"follow\" requests were accepted by Clint. The brand basically grew off just supporters being in the know.\n\nCorteiz's Collaboration with Nike\n\nLast month, Corteiz unveiled its biggest move yet by revealing an upcoming partnership with Nike that includes a pair of Air Max 95s arrived in March. This collaboration marks a significant milestone for the brand and further solidifies its status as a leading streetwear brand.\n\nThe upcoming Aegean Storm will be available in April 2023.\n\nCorteiz's Approach to Releasing Hyped Garments\n\nWhile many successful streetwear labels became infamous for sudden drops with quick sell-out times, Corteiz's approach to releasing hyped garments was distinctively different. Streetwear brands usually carve out a specific day of the week or time for their drops. Instead, Corteiz moves spontaneously. Their drops are cryptically revealed, times are unveiled randomly, and the only way to access the drop is by entering a password.\n\nCorteiz's Brand Philosophy\n\nCorteiz's logo represents how living in society feels like a prison, and the brand is about \"escaping from the societal restraints that we've grown up with to pursue what you really want to do.\" The brand's offerings mostly consist of T-shirts, hoodies, sweatpants, beanies, cargo pants, cargo shorts, and socks with their logos. Their prices range from £12 for a pair of socks and up to £300 for their puffer \"Bolo\" jackets.\n\nThe Future of Corteiz\n\nAs Corteiz continues to grow and gain popularity, it will be interesting to see how the brand's marketing tactics and philosophy evolve. It is clear that the brand has a loyal following that appreciates its unique approach to releasing hyped garments. The partnership with Nike is an exciting milestone for the brand and a sign of things to come. Corteiz is a brand that is definitely worth keeping an eye on in the world of streetwear.",

After letting customers decide what pictures and designs they want on their pieces, Sesay sews what they send in into clothing.\\n\\nSesay has always had an eye for business. When she was younger, she hoped to start her own natural product line for those with curly hair like her, she said. In 2016, her uncle, who was an aspiring fashion designer and music artist, died.         "content": "[{\"docid\": \"72972\", \"url\": \"https://www.nssmag.com/en/fashion/36100/community-fashion-places-faces-corteiz\", \"score\": 0.5958995819091797, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why communities are so important for brands\\nauthor: Author Sagra de Manueles\\ndate: 2024-03-14\\n---\\nWhy communities are so important for brands\\n\\nBorn in the streetwear world, luxury fashion also wants to recreate them\\n\\nMarch 14th, 2024\\n\\nPossessing its own community is something fundamental for any fashion brand - even though the meaning of the word is often ambiguous. In the best cases, a brand's community forms mostly on its own, albeit with the help and encouragement of the brand itself, as is the case with Diesel, for example; there are many others, especially in the luxury field, where the community and the clientele do not always correspond, leading us to speak more of a \\\"following\\\" than a community, which is more artificially constructed through precise marketing strategies. Either way, a community is needed because it constitutes not so much the audience of a brand, but the people who are under its influence. If a certain collection or brand launches a trend that others follow, think of Miu Miu or Balenciaga in recent years, it is the community that acts as a sounding board for it - what in marketing theory is called \\\"early adopters\\\". Communities play a crucial role in defining a brand identity: the progressive ladies of the 1920s were the community of Chanel, just as CEOs and magnates from around the world represent the community of Brunello Cucinelli or Loro Piana, rock singers are the community of any Hedi Slimane project, and career women with an intellectual side are the community of The Row and Phoebe Philo. There is a clear connection, however, betwee\", \"total_chars\": 5831, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"22731\", \"url\": \"https://www.voguebusiness.com/fashion/corteiz-clint-and-the-future-of-streetwear\", \"score\": 0.573395311832428, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why everyone's talking about Corteiz\\nauthor: Kati Chitrakorn\\ndate: 2022-01-31\\n---\\nTo receive the Vogue Business newsletter, sign up here.\\n\\nOn a weekend in January, groups of young people were spotted climbing fences and running through a car park in Wormwood Scrubs, west London, carrying puffer jackets from brands including The North Face, Stussy, Moncler, Supreme and Arc'teryx. Coordinates were shared on social media along with instructions to bring an authentic branded down jacket in reasonable condition. That made you eligible to receive one of Corteiz's new Bolo jackets. Hundreds of young adults showed up, even though the brand had only 50 jackets to give away.\\n\\nCorteiz (also known as Crtz) was launched in 2017. The founder is known publicly as simply Clint. So too, however, are about 400 anxious 13 to 30 year olds, clamoring for the opportunity to give their pants away.\\n\\nAt about 11 a.m. on a block of West Street just south of Greenpoint Avenue, the air fills with the sound of skidding Citi Bike tires and recently released Air Jordans thudding against the pavement. Suddenly, frantically, a line is forming outside a nondescript warehouse. \\\"DA GREAT DENIM EXCHANGE,\\\" a pop-up event orchestrated by British streetwear label Corteiz, is about to begin—and it's bringing a bit of streetwear hysteria into the neighborhood's millennial equanimity.\\n\\nA day earlier, the brand announced via Instagram that in less than 24 hours it would be doing its second-ever event in New York. Crucially, participants were required to wear their (clean) jeans to the event, hand them in, and wa\", \"total_chars\": 10903, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"93766\", \"url\": \"https://moresneakers.com/blog/detail/corteiz:-the-guerilla-streetwear-brand-that-took-over-london\", \"score\": 0.5700938701629639, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Corteiz: The Guerilla Streetwear Brand That Took Over London\\ndate: 2023-04-12\\n---\\nCorteiz's Unconventional Marketing Tactics\\n\\nIn recent years, it has become rarer to see hordes of shoppers mobbing city streets to buy a limited edition drop from any streetwear label. Many streetwear brands have followed the same playbook - design a seasonal collection, schedule an online release date, and continue selling items via stockists or other retail partners. However, there are brands like Corteiz that have employed unconventional guerilla marketing tactics to capture hype and allure unseen within streetwear in some time.\\n\\nFounded in 2017 by Clint Ogbenna, a British-Nigerian entrepreneur, Corteiz RTW (Rules The World) has become one of the most popular streetwear brands to come out of London since Palace. Within the past five years, the brand's logo of Alcatraz Island has blown up and is now spotted everywhere. In addition, some of the biggest celebrities have given their seal of approval to the brand. Recently, Drake was seen sporting a leather jacket that the brand released this winter, and Pharrell invited the brand's founder, Clint, to a private Friendsgiving dinner held at Selfridges last fall.\\n\\nSurprisingly, Corteiz's social media pages were originally private - for a while, new customers could only learn about the brand's latest relea\", \"total_chars\": 3490, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"37360\", \"url\": \"https://ecoaya.com/blogs/sustainability/community-clothing-brand-communities-sustainable-fashion\", \"score\": 0.5627676248550415, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Community Clothing: Redefining Fashion for a Sustainable Future\\ndate: 2024-10-01\\n---\\nCommunity Clothing:\\n\\nRedefining Fashion for a Sustainable Future\\n\\n.\\n\\nAYA | JANUARY 14, 2025\\n\\nREADING TIME: 7 minutes\\n\\nToday, the fashion industry faces challenges not only from the economic and environmental impacts of fast fashion but also from growing ethical debates that influence consumer purchasing behaviors. As these ethical concerns gain prominence, the concept of community clothing has evolved into something far more than just a trend. Community clothing is now a multifaceted approach to fashion, with each initiative having its own unique impact.\\n\\nIn this article, we explore the diverse landscape of community clothing, with a special focus on those that advocate for sustainability and drive positive change.\\n\\nBrand Communities vs. Community Clothing: Unpacking the Connection\\n\\nA concept closely related to community clothing is brand communities, often mistaken for the same thing. The collective value both terms bring to the table lies in the creation of implicit, discursive, and emotional value for consumers [1]. This overlap can create some confusion. Brand communities aim to strengthen the consumer-brand relationship while fostering a sense of loyalty and understanding between consumers and the community [2,3].\\n\\nThis creates a shared identity and a deeper connection with the brand's vision, turning consumers into \\\"co-creators\\\" of the products [3] or, at the very least, making them feel that their voices and desires influence the brand's projects.\\n\\nSo, what exactly is comm\", \"total_chars\": 15642, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"9472\", \"url\": \"https://www.stu.edu/news/flysupply-stu-fashion-collab-launch/\", \"score\": 0.5577812194824219, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: FlySupply & STU Fashion Collab Launch\\ndate: 2023-10-24\\n---\\nFlySupply & STU Fashion Collab Launch\\n\\nby Walter Villa, Special to STU\\n\\nThis was a match made in heaven – literally.\\n\\nSt. Thomas University, a Catholic institution, and Fly Supply, a clothing line with religious messaging, have made a collaboration blessed by the angels.\\n\\nOn Friday afternoon – accented by a live DJ and tasty food and beverages — students and other guests ventured out to the on-campus Fernandez Family Center lobby to enjoy the launch of Fly Supply's STU line. The sporty line, in an array of bright colors, features messages such as:\\n\\n\\\"GOD GOT MY BACK.\\\"\\n\\n\\\"NEVER SOLD MY SOUL.\\\"\\n\\nAnd …\\n\\n\\\"THE DEVIL IS JEALOUS OF ME.\\\"\\n\\nProfessor Ashlee Rzyczycki, the director of STU's fashion merchandising program, said it was in 2021 that she met the four founders of Fly Supply – Garrett Brown, Rick Maxwell, Kevin Pamphile, and Reginald Bourdeau, all of whom are from Miami.\\n\\nProfessor Rzyczycki quickly decided that working with this hip quartet of designers would be a huge win for St. Thomas University in general, and her students in particular.\\n\\n\\\"They have a great brand,\\\" said Professor Rzyczycki, who was introduced to the Fly Supply guys by STU employee Brandon Vega. \\\"I wanted to incorporate that brand into my classroom.\\\"\\n\\nIn that initial meeting, Professor Rzyczycki said she had an \\\"amazing\\\" two-hour conversation with the Fly Supply guys.\\n\\n\\\"Their brand is super successful,\\\" she said. \\\"I knew this collaboration would really resonate with my students.\\\"\\n\\nFly Supply has previously collaborated with Miami Heat leg\", \"total_chars\": 3707, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"89023\", \"url\": \"https://fashionista.com/2020/08/fashion-brands-celebrity-famous-public-facing-founders\", \"score\": 0.5567072033882141, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Does a Fashion Brand Need a Public-Facing Founder to Survive?\\nauthor: Dhani Mau\\ndate: 2020-08-04\\n---\\nDoes a Fashion Brand Need a Public-Facing Founder to Survive?\\n\\nIn the fashion world, there are a smorgasbord of founders and designers we read and hear about. There's the celebrity designer, which could either mean a celebrity-turned-designer or a designer-turned-celebrity; the socialite designer; the influencer designer (again, that could be an influencer-turned-designer or vice versa); the millennial 'Girlboss' founder; the mythical, legendary designer whose name is everywhere but whose personal life and personality we know little about. With decreasing frequency, it seems, there's also the talented, classically trained, dues-paid, behind-the-scenes designer who wants their work to speak for itself.\\n\\nFashion brands have been harnessing the power of celebrity for over a century. Ove\", \"total_chars\": 2997, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"22731\", \"url\": \"https://www.voguebusiness.com/fashion/corteiz-clint-and-the-future-of-streetwear\", \"score\": 0.6766314506530762, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why everyone's talking about Corteiz\\nauthor: Kati Chitrakorn\\ndate: 2022-01-31\\n---\\nTo receive the Vogue Business newsletter, sign up here.\\n\\nOn a weekend in January, groups of young people were spotted climbing fences and running through a car park in Wormwood Scrubs, west London, carrying puffer jackets from brands including The North Face, Stussy, Moncler, Supreme and Arc'teryx. In the best cases, a brand's community forms mostly on its own, albeit with the help and encouragement of the brand itself, as is the case with Diesel, for example; there are many others, especially in the luxury field, where the community and the clientele do not always correspond, leading us to speak more of a \\\"following\\\" than a community, which is more artificially constructed through precise marketing strategies. Either way, a community is needed because it constitutes not so much the audience of a brand, but the people who are under its influence. If a certain collection or brand launches a trend that others follow, think of Miu Miu or Balenciaga in recent years, it is the community that acts as a sounding board for it - what in marketing theory is called \\\"early adopters\\\". \"---\\ntitle: Here's Who Has Gone Public In 2018 (So Far)\\nauthor: Alex Wilhelm\\ndate: 2018-10-03\\n---\\nEarlier this year, it was too early to tell if the 2018 IPO cycle would bear out. After all, the preceding several years had proven to be consistent disappointments when it came to tech startup liquidity. Few startups went public, and a horde of richly-valued unicorns sat on the sidelines simply waiting.\\n\\nHappily, for investors and founders alike, 2018 has produced a host of technology IPOs. In fact, the flow of tech companies going public was a theme in our Q1 venture reporting and our Q2 venture reporting.         "content": "{\"docid\": \"77382\", \"url\": \"https://www.businessofapps.com/data/spotify-statistics/\", \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Spotify Revenue and Usage Statistics (2025)\\ndate: 2025-02-25\\n---\\nSpotify is the world's biggest music streaming platform by number of subscribers. Free Spotify access comes with lower sound quality, advertisements and requires an internet connection. Those who pay for Spotify Premium can listen uninterrupted to high-quality recordings and are able to download songs for offline listening.\\n\\nSpotify was founded in 2006 in Stockholm, Sweden, by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. The two wanted to create a legal digital music platform to respond to growing challenge of online music piracy in the early 2000s.\\n\\nEventually convincing record labels to agree to share content in return for an aggregate 20 percent stake, Spotify was launched in 2008. It was an instant success, with a Facebook partnership helping it rise rapidly to prominence. Surviving the transition to mobile, Spotify went public in April 2018, with a market cap of $26.5 billion after the first day of trading.\\n\\nIt has drawn criticism from recording artists, who complain that it pays too little. Claims to democratize the music industry have also been questioned, with the world's biggest four music labels responsible for 87 percent of content available on Spotify.\\n\\nUnfair or not, with the days of physical music long behind us (with the exception of vinyl junkies), Spotify dominates the way we consume music this century.         "content": "[{\"docid\": \"84696\", \"url\": \"https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2017/03/02/518081927/snapchat-parent-to-begin-trading-on-the-new-york-stock-exchange-thursday\", \"score\": 0.5952717065811157, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Snapchat Parent's Stock Soars By 50 Percent On First Day Of Trading\\nauthor: Doreen McCallister\\ndate: 2017-03-02\\n---\\nSnapchat Parent's Stock Soars By 50 Percent On First Day Of Trading\\n\\nShares of Snap Inc., parent of the popular disappearing-message and camera-centric app Snapchat, rose by more than $8 in the first hours of trading Thursday, as the company watched the $17 price of its initial public offering of 200 million nonvoting shares soar by 50 percent as of mid-day Thursday.\\n\\nThe stock opened above $24 when the new offering began sales shortly after 11 a.m. It then rose above $25 a share, hitting $25.64 by 1:31 p.m.\\n\\nThe initial pricing valued the 5-year-old company, based in Los Angeles, at $24 billion. Earlier projections had expected the range of $14 to $16.\\n\\nLast month, Snap filed paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission to become a publicly traded company.\\n\\nSnap's Snapchat app is best known for disappearing messages and quirky facial filters for jazzing up selfies. It's popular with teenagers and younger millennials.\\n\\nBut despite Snapchat's popularity, user growth has slowed recently.\\n\\nSnapchat started 2017 with 158 million daily active users, most of whom are people in their teens, 20s and early 30s.\\n\\nDoes Snapchat need to go beyond young users to succeed?\\n\\nLaVon Murphy, 45, a photographer in Portland, Ore., told The Associated Press that she uses Snapchat to stay in touch with her 17-year-old son.\\n\\n\\\" 'I don't really understand why he and his friends use the app so extensively, but I am trying to keep up,' she said.\\n\\n\\\" 'It allows me to be\", \"total_chars\": 3113, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"22806\", \"url\": \"https://www.statista.com/statistics/272014/global-social-networks-ranked-by-number-of-users/\", \"score\": 0.53764808177948, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Most used social networks 2025, by number of users\\nauthor: Stacy Jo Dixon; Mar\\ndate: 2025-03-26\\n---\\nMarket leader Facebook was the first social network to surpass one billion registered accounts and currently sits at more than three billion monthly active users. Meta Platforms owns four of the biggest social media platforms, all with more than one billion monthly active users each: Facebook (core platform), WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, and Instagram. In the third quarter of 2023, Facebook reported around four billion monthly core Family product users.\\n\\nThe United States and China account for the most high-profile social platforms\\n\\nMost top ranked social networks with more than 100 million users originated in the United States, but services like Chinese social networks WeChat, QQ or video sharing app Douyin have also garnered mainstream appeal in their respective regions due to local context and content. Douyin's popularity has led to the platform releasing an international version of its network: a little app called TikTok.\\n\\nHow many people use social media?\\n\\nThe leading social networks are usually available in multiple languages and enable users to connect with friends or people across geographical, political, or economic borders. In the best cases, a brand's community forms mostly on its own, albeit with the help and encouragement of the brand itself, as is the case with Diesel, for example; there are many others, especially in the luxury field, where the community and the clientele do not always correspond, leading us to speak more of a \\\"following\\\" than a community, which is more artificially constructed through precise marketing strategies. Either way, a community is needed because it constitutes not so much the audience of a brand, but the people who are under its influence. If a certain collection or brand launches a trend that others follow, think of Miu Miu or Balenciaga in recent years, it is the community that acts as a sounding board for it - what in marketing theory is called \\\"early adopters\\\". Communities play a crucial role in defining a brand identity: the progressive ladies of the 1920s were the community of Chanel, just as CEOs and magnates from around the world represent the community of Brunello Cucinelli or Loro Piana, rock singers are the community of any Hedi Slimane project, and career women with an intellectual side are the community of The Row and Phoebe Philo. There is a clear connection, however, betwee\", \"total_chars\": 5831, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"87070\", \"url\": \"https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbescommunicationscouncil/2024/10/01/the-power-of-community-how-fashion-brands-are-building-loyalty-among-gen-z/\", \"score\": 0.5429238677024841, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: The Power Of Community: How Fashion Brands Are Building Loyalty Among Gen Z\\ndate: 2024-10-01\\n---\\nAlison Bringé is Chief Marketing Officer at Launchmetrics, a leading Brand Performance Cloud in Fashion, Lifestyle and Beauty.\\n\\nWhat do Gen Z consumers want? There are many viable answers to that question, but I'd argue that it has less to do with the products that brands sell and more to do with the feelings they create.\\n\\nGen Zers want to make connections. They want to share and participate—to find meaning in a digital world. In short, they want to belong.\\n\\nFor fashion, lifestyle and beauty brands looking to win over Gen Z's loyalty, this is a crucial thing to understand. Gen Z consumers want to connect with others who share their values; they want to find their tribe—and the brands that succeed are the ones that step in and fill that need in an authentic way.\\n\\nWhy Is Community So Important?\\n\\nBelonging is at the crux of it, but there's more to be said about the importance of community. For one thing, Gen Zers prefer brands with stories; brands that stand for something—brands they can connect to on an emotional level. Purchasing from such brands goes beyond the product: It's a form of self-expression—a badge they wear to publicly demonstrate their values. Building a community around your brand allows Gen Z to know where you stand and to stand with you.\\n\\nAt the same time, the concept of authority has shifted.         "content": "[{\"docid\": \"77382\", \"url\": \"https://www.businessofapps.com/data/spotify-statistics/\", \"score\": 0.6121459007263184, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Spotify Revenue and Usage Statistics (2025)\\ndate: 2025-02-25\\n---\\nSpotify is the world's biggest music streaming platform by number of subscribers. Free Spotify access comes with lower sound quality, advertisements and requires an internet connection. Those who pay for Spotify Premium can listen uninterrupted to high-quality recordings and are able to download songs for offline listening.\\n\\nSpotify was founded in 2006 in Stockholm, Sweden, by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. The two wanted to create a legal digital music platform to respond to growing challenge of online music piracy in the early 2000s.\\n\\nEventually convincing record labels to agree to share content in return for an aggregate 20 percent stake, Spotify was launched in 2008. It was an instant success, with a Facebook partnership helping it rise rapidly to prominence. Surviving the transition to mobile, Spotify went public in April 2018, with a market cap of $26.5 billion after the first day of trading.\\n\\nIt has drawn criticism from recording artists, who complain that it pays too little. Claims to democratize the music industry have also been questioned, with the world's biggest four music labels responsible for 87 percent of content available on Spotify.\\n\\nUnfair or not, with the days of physical music long behind us (with the exception of vinyl junkies), Spotify dominates the way we consume music this century. Now there are 4.26 billion people that use social media worldwide.\\n\\nThat's more than half of the total world population!\\n\\nThe rapid growth in social media usage has completely changed the way we live and interact with each other.\\n\\nBut is this growth starting to slow?\\n\\nI've compiled a list of the latest social media user statistics showing just how big social media has become and where it's likely to go in the future.\\n\\nWhat Will I Learn?\\n\\nBillions of people rely on social media every day.\\n\\nThere are hundreds of social media sites that vary in size and function.\\n\\nThese are the key social media statistics that you need to know:\\n\\n- About 58.4% of the world's population uses social media today\\n\\n- That equates to 4.26 billion people around the world now using social media\\n\\n- The average daily social media usage is 2 hours and 27 minutes\\n\\n- The average social media user has an account on 6.6 social media platforms\\n\\n- Social media has had an average compounded growth rate of 12% since 2012\\n\\n- Social media usage grew at an average rate of 13.5 new users every second throughout 2021\\n\\n- Almost 75% of the world's population over the age of 13+ uses social media in some form\\n\\n- 93% of people who use the internet regularly also use social media\\n\\n- 72% of all Americans actively use social media\\n\\nAs you can see, social media is a big part of\", \"total_chars\": 30552, \"truncated\": true}]"
