        "content": "{\"docid\": \"7940\", \"url\": \"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Francis\", \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Ben Francis - Wikipedia\\ndate: 2020-08-14\\n---\\nname: Ben Francis\\nhonorific_suffix: GBR 100% MBE\\nbirth_name: Benjamin David Francis\\nbirth_date: 04 06 1992\\nbirth_place: West Midlands, England\\neducation: South Bromsgrove High School\\nalma_mater: Aston University (dropped out)\\nknown for: Co-founder, CEO and majority owner of Gymshark\\nspouse: Robin Gallant (m. 2021)\\nchildren: 2\\nwebsite: benfrancis.com\\n\\nBenjamin David Francis (born 4 June 1992) is a British businessman. He is the co-founder, CEO and majority owner of Gymshark, a fitness apparel and accessories company founded in 2012.\\n\\nWith a stake of over 70% in Gymshark which is currently valued by investors at $1.45 billion, Francis had a net worth of $1.3 billion as of April 2023. In April 2023, he made his debut on Forbes' annual The World's Billionaires list as the 2,259th richest person in the world.\\n\\nEarly life\\n\\nBenjamin David Francis was born in the West Midlands, England in 1992 and grew up in Bromsgrove, Worcestershire. He attended South Bromsgrove High School. He first became interested in computing after studying IT at school. His first business was an online company that sold car number plates. Francis started going to the gym as a teenager. He later said \\\"the structure, consistency and work ethic I found in the gym I realised, could be applied to different areas of my life and it would work.\\\" In 2010, he enrolled at Aston University for international business and management wherein he had \\\"a strong foundation on which to build a business.\\\" He dropped out in 2012.\\n\\nCareer\\n\\nBefore launching Gymshark, Francis developed two fitness applications, Fat Loss Abs Guide and . While at university between 2010 and 2013, he worked for Pizza Hut as a delivery boy earning £5 an hour. He left six months after launching Gymshark.\\n\\nGymshark\\n\\nIn 2012, at 19, he launched Gymshark in his parents' garage with school friend Lewis Morgan. The website initially sold fitness supplements. Unable to afford to buy stock or secure distribution deals with supplement suppliers, he began dropshipping supplies from other vendors and it took him six weeks to make his first sale. In 2013, branching out from supplements, Francis began designing and selling fitness apparel on Gymshark's website. He began manufacturing the products from his parents' garage in Bromsgrove, using a sewing machine and screen printer he bought with £1,000 of savings. He learned how to sew from his grandmother.\\n\\nIn 2013, he exhibited Gymshark's products at the BodyPower fitness trade show in Birmingham. After the trade show ended, a tracksuit went viral on Facebook, generating £30,000 in sales within 30 minutes. Francis later left university and quit his job at Pizza Hut to focus on the company full-time. As a start-up, Francis marketed the brand through partnering with social media influencers, including body builders Nikki Blackketter and Lex Griffin. Gymshark was one of the first brands to make extensive use of social media influencers.\\n\\nIn 2015, Francis stepped down as CEO of the company to become chief marketing officer, chief brand officer and chief product officer. At the time, he said the move would allow the company \\\"to grow even more quickly\\\" and give him time to \\\"work on my weaknesses and become a more rounded businessperson\\\". In 2018, Gymshark opened a new £5 million headquarters in Solihull, West Midlands. In 2019, Gymshark opened its own branded gym and innovation hub. Since 2016, Gymshark has been listed on The Sunday Times Fast Track of fast-growing private companies. The company currently sells products in 131 countries.\\n\\nIn August 2020, Gymshark sold a 21% stake to US private equity firm General Atlantic in a deal which valued the company in excess of £1 billion. Francis currently owns more than 70% of the company, which is worth £700 million. In August 2021, he returned to the role of the company's CEO.\\n\\nIn 2018, Francis was included on the Forbes 30 Under 30 list. In 2019, Francis served on the UK Government's Business Council for Entrepreneurs. In 2020, Francis was awarded the EY UK Entrepreneur of the Year Award. Francis was appointed Member of the Order of the British Empire (MBE) in the 2023 New Year Honours for services to the business sector.\\n\\nPersonal life\\n\\nFrancis is a car and motorcycle enthusiast, and a season ticket holder at Aston Villa. He and his girlfriend Robin Gallant became engaged in April 2021, and married on 9 September 2021. On 8 September 2022, Francis announced that they were expecting twins. Their twin sons were born on 24 December 2022. In July 2024, the couple announced that they were expecting another child.\\n\\nReferences\\n\\nCategory:Living people\\nCategory:British online retailer founders\\nCategory:Alumni of Aston University\\nCategory:People from Bromsgrove\\nCategory:Members of the Order of the British Empire\\nCategory:1992 births\", \"offset\": 0, \"total_chars\": 4866, \"truncated\": false, \"next_offset\": null}"

        "content": "{\"docid\": \"19241\", \"url\": \"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandora_(service)\", \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Pandora (service) - Wikipedia\\ndate: 2005-11-28\\n---\\nname: Pandora\\nlogo: Pandora wordmark.svg\\ntype: Music streaming service\\nlocation: Oakland, California, U.S.\\nlocations: 7\\nfounder: Will GlaserJon KraftTim Westergren\\nservices: Internet radio\\nprogramming_language: Java\\nadvertising: Banner ads, video ads, audio ads\\nregistration: Optional (required to save stations)\\ncompany_type: Subsidiary\\nlanguage: English\\nnative_clients: Universal Windows App, iOS, Android\\nfoundation: 2000 (as Savage Beast Technologies)Oakland, California, U.S.\\narea_served: United States\\nnum_employees: 1, 938 (2019)Pandora Media LLC Company Profile Bloomberg Markets July 21, 2020\\nparent: Sirius XM (2019–present)\\nsubsidiaries: Rdio (as of December 22, 2015), Next Big Sound (as of November 1, 2021) Adswizz (as of May 29, 2018) Stitcher (as of August 29, 2023)\\nnum_users: 55.9 million active (2021), Pandora ended Q1 2021 with 55.9m monthly active listeners - Music Ally April 29, 2021 6.4 million subscribers (2021) Pandora ended Q1 2021 with 55.9m monthly active listeners - Music Ally April 29, 2021\\ncurrent_status: Active\\nfootnotes: 2019 Form 10-K Annual Report SiriusXM Holdings July 21, 2020\\n\\nPandora is a subscription-based music streaming service owned by the broadcasting corporation Sirius XM that is based in Oakland, California in the United States. The service carries a focus on recommendations based on the \\\"Music Genome Project\\\", which is a means of classifying individual songs by musical traits such as genres and shared instrumentation. The service originally launched in the consumer market as an internet radio service that would generate personalized channels based on these traits as well as specific tracks liked by the user; this service is available in an advertising-supported tier and additionally a subscription-based version. In 2017, the service launched Pandora Premium, which is an on-demand version of the service more in line with contemporary competitors.\\n\\nThe company was founded in 2000 as Savage Beast Technologies, and initially conceived as a business-to-business company licensing the Music Genome Project to retailers as a recommendation platform. In 2005, the company shifted its focus to the consumer market by launching Pandora as an internet radio product. Pandora is a freemium service; basic features are free with advertisements or limitations, while additional features, such as improved streaming quality, music downloads and offline channels are offered via paid subscriptions.\\n\\nIn February 2019, Sirius XM acquired Pandora for $3.5 billion in stock. In 2021, Pandora had about 55.9 million active monthly users, and 6.4 million subscribers. , Pandora reportedly had fewer than 50 million active users. As of 2023, there were 46 million users.\\n\\nHistory\\n\\nEarly history\\n\\nIn 2000, Will Glaser, Jon Kraft, and Tim Westergren founded the company as Savage Beast Technologies. Will Glaser had conceptualized the concept of classifying music by various traits and attributes—an effort that he would later name the \\\"Music Genome Project\\\". The company was originally pitched as an e-commerce service that would use Glaser's associated algorithm as a recommendation engine, but this idea was scrapped after the Dot-com bubble hit its peak in March 2000. Afterwards, the company pursued licensing the technology to other retailers, such as AOL Music and Best Buy (who used it for in-store kiosks as a trial).\\n\\nThe company faced increasing debt, and ran through its initial $2 million in funding by 2001. Glaser, Kraft, and Westergren then convinced Savage Beast's 50 employees to work for two years without pay, prompting a lawsuit by former employees in 2003 due to deferred salaries being illegal under California law. After settling the suit, just a few employees were laid off. In 2004, based on the success of the Best Buy pilot, Walden Venture Capital led an $8 million round of funding, and hired Joe Kennedy—formerly of automaker Saturn—as its new CEO. After agreements with Best Buy and Borders lapsed, the company began to shift its attention to the consumer market, resulting in the development of Pandora as an internet radio service using the Music Genome Project as a personalization system.\\n\\nAfter a beta period, Pandora officially launched in August 2005. Upon its launch, it was a subscription-based service, but added a free, ad-supported version in November after Westergren realized users were abusing its 10-hour free trial by making new e-mail addresses. Advertising could also be targeted based on the current song.\\n\\nGrowth\\n\\nIn 2011, Pandora went public via an initial public offering on the New York Stock Exchange. At the time, Pandora had 800,000 tracks from 80,000 artists in its library and 80 million users. As of end of mid-year 2018, Pandora had 71.4 million active users.\\n\\nOn March 7, 2013, Pandora chairman and chief executive officer Joseph J. Kennedy announced that he would leave the company after nine years.\\n\\nIn April 2013, Pandora announced that its radio streaming service had 200 million users, including 70 million monthly active users. By December 2013, Pandora accounted for 70% of all internet radio listening in the United States.\\n\\nOn September 1, 2013, Pandora removed a 40-hour-per-month limitation for free mobile listening. As of October 2014, less than 5 percent of active listeners were paying subscribers.\\n\\nBy November 2014, Pandora had approximately doubled its library size, topping 1.5 million songs.\\n\\nOn September 15, 2016, Pandora launched \\\"Pandora Plus\\\", a new $4.99 subscription service to compete with other streaming services.\\n\\nIn early 2017, Pandora revealed that 56 million of its 81 million active users subscribed to the Today's Country station and that country music had accounted for more than 1.7 billion listening hours on the platform in 2016.\\n\\nOn July 31, 2017, Pandora discontinued services in Australia and New Zealand, citing a need to focus solely on the U.S. market.\\n\\nIn September 2017, Roger Lync\", \"offset\": 0, \"total_chars\": 25508, \"truncated\": true, \"next_offset\": 6000}"

\"---\\ntitle: Number of ChatGPT Users (March 2025)\\nauthor: Fabio Duarte\\ndate: 2025-06-05\\n---\\nNumber of ChatGPT Users (March 2025)\\n\\nOpenAI's ChatGPT took off in record-breaking It plans to hit 1 billion users by the end of 2025.\\n\\n| Month | Weekly Users |\\n\\n| November 2022 | 1 million |\\n\\n| January 2023 | 30 million |\\n\\n| November 2023 | 100 million |\\n\\n| December 2024 | 300 million |\\n\\n| February 2025 | 400 million |\\n\\nSources: Reuters, Semrush, CNBC, The Verge, Techerati\\n\\nChatGPT User Demographics\\n\\n64.32% of ChatGPT users are male, and 35.68% are female.\\n\\nMore than 45% of its users are under the age of 25.\\n\\nSourc\", \"total_chars\": 10477, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"22806\", \"url\": \"https://www.statista.com/statistics/272014/global-social-networks-ranked-by-number-of-users/\", \"score\": 0.5200275182723999, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Most used social networks 2025, by number of users\\nauthor: Stacy Jo Dixon; Mar\\ndate: 2025-03-26\\n---\\nMarket leader Facebook was the first social network to surpass one billion registered accounts and currently sits at more than three billion monthly active users. Meta Platforms owns four of the biggest social media platforms, all with more than one billion monthly active users each: Facebook (core platform), WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, and Instagram. In the third quarter of 2023, Facebook reported around four billion monthly core Family product users.\\n\\nThe United States and China account for the most high-profile social platforms\\n\\nMost top ranked social networks with more than 100 million users originated in the United States, but services like Chinese social networks WeChat, QQ or video sharing app Douyin have also garnered mainstream appeal in their respective regions due to local context and content. Douyin's popularity has led to the platform releasing an international version of its network: a little app called TikTok.\\n\\nHow many people use social media?\\n\\nThe leading social networks are usually available in multiple languages and enable users to connect with friends or people across geographical, political, or economic borders. So they launched a fashion line dedicated to casual clothing for work.\\nauthor: Molly Callahan\\ndate: 2019-02-27\\n---\\nThey couldn't find anything to wear in New Delhi. So they launched a fashion line dedicated to casual clothing for work.\\n\\nAashray Thatai and Ashish Gurnani were frustrated. They were each working full time in professional settings near New Delhi, and couldn't find clothes that were stylish, affordable, and appropriate both for work and dinner afterward. Ove\", \"total_chars\": 2997, \"truncated\": true}, {\"docid\": \"22731\", \"url\": \"https://www.voguebusiness.com/fashion/corteiz-clint-and-the-future-of-streetwear\", \"score\": 0.6884253025054932, \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why everyone's talking about Corteiz\\nauthor: Kati Chitrakorn\\ndate: 2022-01-31\\n---\\nTo receive the Vogue Business newsletter, sign up here.\\n\\nOn a weekend in January, groups of young people were spotted climbing fences and running through a car park in Wormwood Scrubs, west London, carrying puffer jackets from brands including The North Face, Stussy, Moncler, Supreme and Arc'teryx. In the best cases, a brand's community forms mostly on its own, albeit with the help and encouragement of the brand itself, as is the case with Diesel, for example; there are many others, especially in the luxury field, where the community and the clientele do not always correspond, leading us to speak more of a \\\"following\\\" than a community, which is more artificially constructed through precise marketing strategies. Either way, a community is needed because it constitutes not so much the audience of a brand, but the people who are under its influence. If a certain collection or brand launches a trend that others follow, think of Miu Miu or Balenciaga in recent years, it is the community that acts as a sounding board for it - what in marketing theory is called \\\"early adopters\\\". Communities play a crucial role in defining a brand identity: the progressive ladies of the 1920s were the community of Chanel, just as CEOs and magnates from around the world represent the community of Brunello Cucinelli or Loro Piana, rock singers are the community of any Hedi Slimane project, and career women with an intellectual side are the community of The Row and Phoebe Philo. They were raised learning martial arts and studying the art of warfare, and created a large army of rebels—mostly women, according to popular legends. Unfortunately, when the Chinese attacked them again three years later with a massive army, they were soundly defeated. Instead of being taken prisoner, Trac and Nhi drowned themselves in the Hat River. They are now regarded as national heroines of Vietnam, and temples throughout the country are dedicated to their memory.\\n\\n2.         "content": "{\"docid\": \"86532\", \"url\": \"https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5f02f6f3ff3ad26698daa428/t/659d1f585999ca03a3779b50/1704795995101/Corteiz%2B%281%29.pdf\", \"text\": \"re notorious for hosting events where they giveaway some stock. Clink often posts his live location on his socials where he'll give away some items to the first few to arrive. Giveaways help to increase brand recognition which encourages people to buy, the more someone notices a name the more they likely to trust it . It's thought on average 34% of new customers are acquired through giveaways and competitions . The more memorable your promotions are the more sales you are able to drive . This is what Corteiz are the kings at, holding numerous crazy events. Here are a few examples of the best:.\\nSocial Media Presence As previously mentioned, the website is password protected but their Instagram page is also private. This means people cannot simply browse the brand, which goes against natural instinct when trying to increase brand exposure. However, it creates a community feel as you have to be accepted in, keeping customers close. Clint has said he wants Corteiz to feel like a \\\"private club that everyone wants to join\\\" and this really cements that .\\nAs seen in figure 7, the creative director has a massive influence on customer perception of a brand. Clint is blunt and nonchalant but very active on his socials. He replies to a lot of DMs and tweets things like \\\"how do you formally tell someone to suck their mum in an email\\\". Despite this being rude and probably no.1 in the How Not to be a CEO Guide it makes him much more personable and relatable. Reportedly 76% of people who feel connected to a brand are more likely to buy from it over competitors and this social presence really makes Corteiz stand out from the rest .\\n+34% Average percentage of new customers acquired through contests \\\"Da Great Bolo Exchange\\\" In January 2022 Corteiz were about to release a puffer jacket – the \\\"Bolo\\\" puffer.\\nTo build excitement, Clint threw \\\"Da Great Bolo Exchange\\\". He tweeted out \\\"All the people who've had their norfy for 3 years+ & it's been ran tru, battered and bruised. Tomorrow is your time to redeem it for something that will keep you warmer, satisfied & drippier. 50 Bolo's only. Safe.\\\" before releasing the location . The first 50 people to arrive would get the new coat for free, all they had to do was exchange a puffer jacket in return. The result was insane, with people willing exchanging Moncler and Canada Goose jackets which both sell for north of £1000 . From the 50 jackets, Corteiz raised over £16,000 worth of jackets which they donated to a homeless charity . The Bolo jackets were released on the website soon after for just £180 and sold out in minutes.\\n\\\"99p Store\\\" At the twilight of 2022, the pound was crashing and the whole UK was in a cost of living crisis. Step forward the Corteiz 99p store. Clint tweeted out the coordinates of a shop in Shepherd's Bush and instructed to people to bring exact change. Over 3000 people turned up, the Corteiz crew then gave out tickets at random which granted people access to the store and gave customers the chance to buy a pair of cargos, which retail at £120, for just 99p . No change was given so if people didn't have exactly 99p they couldn't purchase anything.\\n\\\"Crossbar Challenge\\\" Corteiz have just announced their latest event. They posted a promo video with Real Madrid ace Eduardo Camavinga. In the video, Camavinga is seen sporting the latest Corteiz gear and hitting the crossbar from over the halfway line. The Frenchman has also been dubbed over by Clint, so he appears to have an authentic London accent . On the day, the location will be revealed and customers will need to hit the crossbar from outside the 18 yard box to win some free items.\\nWhen consumers feel connected to the brand: 57% Of customers will increase their spending with the brand 76% Will buy the brand over its competitors Figure 13: Clint with jackets handed in Figure 14: Clint at 99p store Fighting Resell With the limited stock model that the streetwear industry tends to use, the resale market has also boomed. Platforms like StockX and Depop have had meteoric rises in recent years. According to PwC's survey, only 33.4% of customers have never bought an item from a reseller . The sentiment behind reselling is positive, it allows consumers to pass on pre-loved items for a bit of cash and reduces the amount of clothes thrown away. The issues come when people buy products just to sell them on for more money, or even sell fakes. It can price out real fans from owning the pieces they want. People have also created bots which automatically buy products for you. . Most brands do nothing about the issue as it ultimately creates them more hype. Corteiz deploy a few tactics to counter the issue as they don't want there to be a financial barrier as this would jeopardise the community aspect. Clint frequently posts videos of him cancelling orders if he sees people trying to sell items on Depop that haven't even been shipped yet . Lots of brands use QR verification labels in their products so users can tell they are real. Corteiz have never done this to reduce risk of resale. The only way to really know if a Corteiz item is real is to buy it direct so people will be more cautious buying from third parties.\\nFigure 15: Certilogo label in Stone Island jumperCritique Potential Improvements Corteiz have cemented themselves as on of the best up-and-coming brands in the market. But lots of brands have been here previously and popularity eventually wanes if you keep doing the same thing. Here are a few ways Corteiz can expand the brand into the next phase.\\nInternational Expansion Corteiz have started to gain a small amount international recognition, even holding recent giveaways in Lagos and Sydney . But the brand is still very UK centric with designs inspired by London culture. Whilst some people internationally will believe in the brand image and message, it will be hard to break the international markets with current model. One way to get around this could be by almost franchising the brand. Clint could invest in young, up-and-coming designers to start they own line of Corteiz. For instance there could be a Corteiz New York or Corteiz Paris etc. They would need to instil the same authenticity and message so the product still felt Corteiz, but it would allow them to create designs that are better suited their culture. This would keep the brand feeling underground and like a community, one the factors that makes them stand out. If done right, it could have the same popularity in these new cities as it did in London.\\nThis could unlock the Asian market for Corteiz. There has been a rise in rap and hip-hop music is Asia in recent years, with the birth of TV programmes like \\\"The Rap of China\\\", which has subsequently caused a massive demand for streetwear . It's reported that the average Asian consumer spends roughly 5 times more a month on streetwear products than North American or European shoppers . With over 400 million young people in China alone, there's a huge untapped market that Corteiz could look to break into . Getting in early and being one of the founding brands could allow Corteiz to sculpt the market and land them massive rewards.\\nLondon Paris Toronto New York Lagos Rio de Janeiro Tokyo Sydney LA Figure 16: Map of possible Corteiz designer locations Nike then confirmed the project on their socials and projected the Nike Swoosh alongside the Corteiz insignia onto the store. The hype boomed with streetwear website Hypebeast claiming it will be \\\"one of the most high-profile releases\\\" of the year . What's made it so successful is the fact Nike is seen as one of the biggest brands in the industry, but also that Corteiz seems to have taken the lead on the project. The marketing was done in a Corteiz manner and the pieces don't look out of place with the rest of the brand's stock. Meaning the project feels very in keeping with the brand's message, and the Nike swoosh is just the icing on the cake. Corteiz should do more collabs going forward but they need to make sure they hand-pick the other entities and make sure the items feel real to the Corteiz DNA. This way fans will stay invested and not just think it's a money making scheme. Here are a few examples of collabs I feel would be successful for the brand: Corteiz X Stone Island – High-low collabs mixing luxury with retail has been around for years. It creates more affordable luxury pieces, targeting the aspirational market who perhaps cannot usually afford to shop at these places . It's a strategy used in streetwear successfully before in projects like Supreme & Louis Vuitton. Stone Island is an Italian brand that is considered unclassifiable, sitting somewhere in between streetwear and high fashion. Their designs don't conform to trends and the brand became synonymous with football hooligans . The message is therefore all about defiance and rebellion, making them a perfect partner for Corteiz.\\nCorteiz x Dave – Musical artists hold a big influence on the fashion scene so collabing with Dave, one of the UK's most streamed artists, could have great potential. Dave himself is a fan of Corteiz, even wearing it in his recent music video \\\"Starlight\\\" and releases clothing with albums that always sell well.\\nCorteiz X Casio – Projects that bring brands away from their usual products also tend to do well. The randomness and element of surprise can garner attention as people are interested to see exactly what will be produced. The digital gold Casio watch has risen back in popularity in recent years and became infamous in the UK with the release of comedy series #HoodDocumentary back in 2015. In which, character \\\"Roll Safe\\\" is a rapper who wore and even rapped about his Casio. Therefore this is a fun project I think would do well.\\nCollaborations Collaborations are one of the most common ways in the industry to create buzz. One of the most notorious examples being Nike and Michael Jordan teaming up to create one of the best selling shoe lines of all time, the Nike Air Jordans. If done correctly, they can bridge together two different consumer markets or make some really sort after pieces when two similar brands/people work together . Corteiz have largely been a single entity. Until January 2023, when Corteiz announced an upcoming project with Nike. It was announced in dramatic fashion with the Corteiz Alcatraz logo being projected onto the front of Nike's Oxford Street store . At first many people thought is was just another Clint marketing stunt as Nike had yet to confirm anything and had previously attempted to sue Corteiz due to the naming similarity with their shoe, Nike Cortez . Over the next few days, spraypainted soles of Nike Air Max 95's with the Corteiz 'C' started to appear around London hinting at a Corteiz version of the beloved shoe.\\nFigure 17: Clint on Oxford Street with Corteiz projected onto Niketown Figure 18: Graffiti Air Max 95 sole seen around London Breaking Into Footwear The sneaker industry is massive, worth around $86 billion in 2022 and consistently growing (shown in figure 19) . Sneakers are also the most frequently purchased item with 61.7% of streetwear consumers saying they are more likely to buy shoes than any other item . Corteiz currently do not make their own footwear so this could be a big growth opportunity. It's an even harder industry to break into than fashion due to long manufacturing times and brand heritage being a dominant factor in customer choice.\\nOne way Corteiz could get a grasp of the market is by offering shoes that are seen as Nike Jordan 1's RRP: £180 Off White Out of Office RRP: £460 BAPE Sta RRP: £279 Nike Air Force 1 RRP: £99 +156% +182% 34.2 37.6 41.8 47.7 54.1 58.9 64.3 69.6 70.7 78.5 85.5 91.6 97.2 102.7 2012 2013 2014 2015 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 Sneaker Market Worth in Billions U.S. $ premium versions of fan favourite silhouettes. It's a strategy that is used to great effect by companies like BAPE and Off White.         "content": "{\"docid\": \"86532\", \"url\": \"https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5f02f6f3ff3ad26698daa428/t/659d1f585999ca03a3779b50/1704795995101/Corteiz%2B%281%29.pdf\", \"text\": \"een as legally different designs, but enough similarities that consumers know if they like the standard versions they will like these too. They can also charge more for them.\\nFigure 19: Graph showing the growth sneaker market worth Figure 20: Showing BAPE and Off White shoes, the Nike silhouettes they mimic and the price mock-up Flagship Stores E-commerce shopping has been on the rise for a while now. It's a trend that was only accelerated by COVID. It's thought as much as 52% of UK clothing sales where done online in 2022 . Despite the growing online market, a lot of consumers still value the presence of a brick and mortar store (as seen in figure 7). Opening a London store could help expand Corteiz. Firstly it gives them another channel. Competitors Palace and Supreme both have flagship stores in Soho, London. Day-to-day these are more similar to Apple stores than traditional clothing shops. Due to the drop model, they will only have a few racks of unsold stock. However it allows them to offer more of a customer experience by showing promotional videos and artistic exhibitions. On release days is where a physical shop can really help. The shop layout will transform to a more traditional shop floor, stocked with all the new items. Queues will form long before opening times. Other pedestrians that pass by will wonder what all the commotion is about and will be more likely to ask or research. This helps to spread the brand's name to more people and could result in more customers.\\nIf the store was opened near competitors, consumers who like these brands are more likely to check Corteiz out whilst they're in the area also.\\nFigure 21: Image of customised water fountain inside Palace's New York shop Diversifying the Stock Streetwear is considered more like a leg of fashion rather than a trend . Because of this it is unlikely it will ever completely fall out of the market, but like anything in fashion, popularity rises and falls so there will come a time when streetwear pieces are less sought after. To ensure Corteiz are able to keep an audience in a potentially different market, they should diversify their stock by offering a greater range of products. This doesn't mean they should change all their designs, just having one or two pieces each drop would suffice. This is potentially something Clint is already thinking about as recent \\\"Da Skydive\\\" jacket had a different feel to what we were used to. It had insanely high quality leather with an embossed logo on the back and front.\\nThe jacket retailed at £750 which is vastly different to the usual Corteiz pieces, but still a lot cheaper than competitors like Avirex who sell very similar designs for around £1200 . It takes a step towards the luxury market which is what Corteiz could look at. Having pieces that fall in the grey area between streetwear and high-fashion will be best for longevity and covers them against potential trend shifts. It's evidently a style and market Clint is personally interested in. He often wears bespoke Corteiz products that fall into this category. A lot of consumers follow brands because of the creative director (figure 7) and this is very prevalent with Corteiz as Clint's personal Instagram has nearly 300k followers . Therefore people would know Clint is still releasing want he wants and not conforming to the industry, thus the authenticity behind the brand would still be present. Clint should look at brands like Kith and Represent for inspiration. Both brands are appreciated and worn by streetwear consumers but sit slightly more on the peripherals of the scene. Kith are actually considered one of the OGs in streetwear but now describe themselves as a lifestyle brand, not tying themselves down to a genre . Their pieces are of high quality and tend to have embroidered graphics instead of screen-prints.\\nThey are priced slightly higher than Corteiz, but not in a completely different world with t-shirts being £60-£80 and hoodies retailing around £150. I don't think the price increase would be an issue as long as the quality is reflected and the majority of the drop is kept at current prices. Consumers would see these pieces as special so would understand the price change. \\\"Da Skydive\\\" jacket still sold out in minutes regardless. Despite its popularity, Corteiz has garnered a few haters along the way saying the brand just screen-print, this shift would silence these critics. As mentioned, diversifying the stock covers the brand from potential market changes and improves their longevity. It would also have the instant advantage of increasing brand reach by appealing to a slightly different and older market, with the majority of Kith and Represent's customers falling in the 25-31 category (31.99% and 31.51% respectively) .\\nFigure 23: Clint wearing bespoke Corteiz denim pieces Figure 22: Da Skydive jacket alongside an Avirex jacket Chitrakorn, C. 2022.         "content": "{\"docid\": \"22731\", \"url\": \"https://www.voguebusiness.com/fashion/corteiz-clint-and-the-future-of-streetwear\", \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Why everyone's talking about Corteiz\\nauthor: Kati Chitrakorn\\ndate: 2022-01-31\\n---\\nTo receive the Vogue Business newsletter, sign up here.\\n\\nOn a weekend in January, groups of young people were spotted climbing fences and running through a car park in Wormwood Scrubs, west London, carrying puffer jackets from brands including The North Face, Stussy, Moncler, Supreme and Arc'teryx. They were following clues to take part in Da Great Bolo Exchange, an event organised by London-based streetwear brand Corteiz. Coordinates were shared on social media along with instructions to bring an authentic branded down jacket in reasonable condition. That made you eligible to receive one of Corteiz's new Bolo jackets. Hundreds of young adults showed up, even though the brand had only 50 jackets to give away.\\n\\nCorteiz (also known as Crtz) was launched in 2017. The founder is known publicly as simply Clint. His pieces — including £30 t-shirts, £120 joggers and £125 cargos — feature a distinctive Alcatraz logo that represents rebellion against convention, considered the core message behind the brand.\\n\\nPieces tend to sell out within minutes. The brand produces a limited run of each product, sold via a private e-commerce site (only those selected are granted access via a password) or at a surprise drop in the physical world. The Instagram account is also private. Resale is discouraged by Corteiz, but difficult to enforce — Bolo jackets are retailing on Depop for £500.\\n\\nClint himself declined to speak with Vogue Business for this story and rarely speaks to press, but it's important not to overlook how this brand, and its hugely engaged community, is evolving. Corteiz is a new kind of modern streetwear brand that is keen to set itself apart from other players in a global streetwear industry worth $185 billion, according to PWC, with an egalitarian attitude and tight-knit community drawn to the anti-establishment ethos. A January tweet to tease the event read: \\\"All the people who've had their norfy for 3 years+ & its been ran tru, battered and bruised. Tomorrow is your time to redeem it for something that will keep you warmer, satisfied & drippier. 50 Bolo's only. Safe.\\\"\\n\\nCorteiz is tapping into a sector that has lost touch with its origins in a drive to make money, according to Laura Leeb, a director at PWC's strategy consulting arm Strategy& and author of the company's Streetwear: The New Exclusivity report. Counter-cultural authenticity has been replaced by the commercial imperatives of a multi-billion dollar retail market for the under-25s, she says.\\n\\nThe rise of secondhand channels like StockX, Grailed and Goat has also nurtured a $36 billion resale industry where consumers can make money from selling rare, limited-edition sneakers and other collectible pieces. The market is expected to more than double to $77 billion in the next five years, according to 2021 data from Thredup. Streetwear has become mass, says Leeb. \\\"Many luxury brands are redefining themselves as streetwear brands – and existing players like Supreme have gotten massive due to acquisitions.\\\"\\n\\nThis is not Clint's first brand. A predecessor to Corteiz was Cade, which he founded in 2015 with his friend Ade Sanusi at the age of 19. Both were part of Apex, a London-based collective of creative teenagers who bonded over self expression and personal style while maintaining an IDGAF attitude. It's unclear when the brand stopped operating.\\n\\nCorteiz has over 190,000 followers on Instagram and more than 32,700 on Twitter. In January 2022, it was one of the most searched-for brands in the UK on Depop, with its joggers particularly popular. The brand's fans included the late Virgil Abloh, founder of streetwear brand Off-White and artistic director of Louis Vuitton menswear, who wore Corteiz's \\\"Rules The World\\\" socks to the Met Gala in September 2021, as well as influential British music artists such as Slowthai, Jorja Smith, KwolleM and Central Cee.\\n\\nConnecting with fans\\n\\nThe Corteiz fandom is spectacular, observers say. \\\"I haven't seen that in fashion in a long time,\\\" says Cody Eastmond, who has worked on digital marketing campaigns at creative agency Science Magic with brands such as Glossier and Versace. \\\"Supreme had some of that — where people would sit outside and wait to get into the store. But, many streetwear brands have matured and lost that locality.\\\"\\n\\nDarnell Ferguson documents Corteiz's drops on his YouTube account Darnell Vlogs, which has 58,000 subscribers, and Instagram account @dvrnsz with over 19,000 followers. \\\"I've seen the hype… People were missing work to come and swap their jackets, without the guarantee of even getting a coat,\\\" he says. \\\"I haven't seen another brand do something quite like what Corteiz is doing.\\\"\\n\\nAuthenticity is core to the brand message of Corteiz, which is marketed only through social media, standing out in contrast to the heavy marketing spend of mainstream streetwear brands. \\\"Corteiz doesn't gift people or pay for promotions, so the celebrities you see rocking it have believed in it,\\\" says Sandy Kaur, the London-based entrepreneur behind the platform and podcast Her Story In Sneakers, who first discovered Corteiz through the sneaker community in 2019. \\\"The garms are high quality but they aren't gentrified. The company is Black-owned and very much stands for London culture. It's an 'if-you-know-you-know' brand when you wear it out and about.\\\"\\n\\nWhy does this matter? \\\"Buying from Crtz allows people to feel like they're part of a community,\\\" says Kaur. \\\"I mean, Central Cee wore a full Crtz fit to the Louis Vuitton fashion show and didn't look out of place. That has to count for something, right?\\\"\\n\\nThe feeling of connectivity matters intensely to many younger consumers who are still exploring and developing their personalities, says Pavel Dler, founder and chief executive of youth media company Culted. \\\"There's a gap in the market for brands that make you feel like you belong. Brands often struggle to authentically connect with young fashion and streetwear enthusiasts because they fail to be transparent about their values and contribution towards communities that they're trying to reach,\\\" he explains. \\\"Corteiz does all of these things without even trying. It's just clothes, made by the community for the community, in a way that brings them together.\\\"\\n\\nStreetwear's assimilation into the mainstream\\n\\nAs traditional marketing loses traction with younger consumers, some fashion brands have experimented with streetwear-style drops to create hype. Specialist streetwear designers are being courted. In January, Swiss luxury brand Bally named 29-year-old Rhuigi Villaseñor, founder of streetwear brand Rhude, as its new creative director. In a series of appointments in 2021, LVMH made A Bathing Ape founder Nigo creative director of Kenzo; Gap struck a 10-year-deal for a Yeezy partnership with Kanye West; and J Crew hired as its new creative director Brendon Babenzien, former creative director of Supreme and founder of streetwear label Noah.\\n\\nThe challenge for the streetwear industry is to stay true to its original roots, says Culted's Dler. \\\"In recent years it has been commodified and glamourised. It's been boxed and labelled as one thing, but it's bigger and more fluid than that.\\\"\\n\\nCorteiz returns to streetwear's beginnings, observes Felix Katt, engagement manager at PWC's Strategy&. \\\"The underlying theme here is accessibility and non-conformity. It's not about whether you're wealthy and can afford it, but rather it's about being part of the community and therefore being in the know,\\\" he says.\\n\\nYounger fans are receptive, Eastmond observes. \\\"They're used to this behaviour. There are Discord and Reddit forums where people share information on how to get access. For brands, it's about knowing your audience and how to communicate with them.\\\"\\n\\nSocial responsibility initiatives appeal to this community. The January down jacket swap event had a surprising charitable twist. Three days later, Clint revealed that all the jackets were donated to St Laurence's Larder, a London-based organisation that provides meals for the homeless and those in need. \\\"I've recently seen more environmental, social and governance (ESG) campaigns,\\\" says Strategy&'s Katt. \\\"That makes sense because streetwear is about being in touch with a brand that aligns with your personal values. It's a new undercurrent in streetwear that I personally didn't see two or three years ago.\\\"\\n\\nCould Corteiz lead a return to a more authentic kind of streetwear? \\\"Corporations and fashion houses have profited from a culture that was never really theirs, and the only place streetwear can really head next is returning to where it originated,\\\" says entrepreneur Kaur. \\\"Corteiz is hot right now due to the noise it made, but it will survive beyond being a trend because its core base never relied on the support of the masses. Corteiz isn't hype — it's London.\\\"\\n\\nClarification: Removes full name of Clint per request of the founder due to safety concerns. (31 January 2022)\\n\\nComments, questions or feedback? Email us at feedback@voguebusiness.com.\\n\\nWhat the Supreme VF deal means for streetwear\", \"offset\": 0, \"total_chars\": 9174, \"truncated\": false, \"next_offset\": null}"
      },

        "role": "tool",
        "tool_call_id": "call_03_gkofXIEJbKKKSTr2Dacz0434",
        "content": "{\"docid\": \"93766\", \"url\": \"https://moresneakers.com/blog/detail/corteiz:-the-guerilla-streetwear-brand-that-took-over-london\", \"text\": \"---\\ntitle: Corteiz: The Guerilla Streetwear Brand That Took Over London\\ndate: 2023-04-12\\n---\\nCorteiz's Unconventional Marketing Tactics\\n\\nIn recent years, it has become rarer to see hordes of shoppers mobbing city streets to buy a limited edition drop from any streetwear label. Many streetwear brands have followed the same playbook - design a seasonal collection, schedule an online release date, and continue selling items via stockists or other retail partners. However, there are brands like Corteiz that have employed unconventional guerilla marketing tactics to capture hype and allure unseen within streetwear in some time.\\n\\nFounded in 2017 by Clint Ogbenna, a British-Nigerian entrepreneur, Corteiz RTW (Rules The World) has become one of the most popular streetwear brands to come out of London since Palace. Within the past five years, the brand's logo of Alcatraz Island has blown up and is now spotted everywhere. The brand's garments have been frequently sighted on UK rap stars such as Central Cee, slowthai, Stormzy, and Dave.\\n\\nCorteiz has gained recognition for its garments among UK rap stars including Central Cee, slowthai, Stormzy, and Dave. In addition, some of the biggest celebrities have given their seal of approval to the brand. Recently, Drake was seen sporting a leather jacket that the brand released this winter, and Pharrell invited the brand's founder, Clint, to a private Friendsgiving dinner held at Selfridges last fall.\\n\\nSurprisingly, Corteiz's social media pages were originally private - for a while, new customers could only learn about the brand's latest releases if their \\\"follow\\\" requests were accepted by Clint. The brand basically grew off just supporters being in the know.\\n\\nCorteiz's Collaboration with Nike\\n\\nLast month, Corteiz unveiled its biggest move yet by revealing an upcoming partnership with Nike that includes a pair of Air Max 95s arrived in March. This collaboration marks a significant milestone for the brand and further solidifies its status as a leading streetwear brand.\\n\\nThe upcoming Aegean Storm will be available in April 2023.\\n\\nCorteiz's Approach to Releasing Hyped Garments\\n\\nWhile many successful streetwear labels became infamous for sudden drops with quick sell-out times, Corteiz's approach to releasing hyped garments was distinctively different. Streetwear brands usually carve out a specific day of the week or time for their drops. Instead, Corteiz moves spontaneously. Their drops are cryptically revealed, times are unveiled randomly, and the only way to access the drop is by entering a password.\\n\\nCorteiz's Brand Philosophy\\n\\nCorteiz's logo represents how living in society feels like a prison, and the brand is about \\\"escaping from the societal restraints that we've grown up with to pursue what you really want to do.\\\" The brand's offerings mostly consist of T-shirts, hoodies, sweatpants, beanies, cargo pants, cargo shorts, and socks with their logos. Their prices range from £12 for a pair of socks and up to £300 for their puffer \\\"Bolo\\\" jackets.\\n\\nThe Future of Corteiz\\n\\nAs Corteiz continues to grow and gain popularity, it will be interesting to see how the brand's marketing tactics and philosophy evolve. It is clear that the brand has a loyal following that appreciates its unique approach to releasing hyped garments. The partnership with Nike is an exciting milestone for the brand and a sign of things to come. Corteiz is a brand that is definitely worth keeping an eye on in the world of streetwear.\", \"offset\": 0, \"total_chars\": 3490, \"truncated\": false, \"next_offset\": null}"
      },
